This is not a certification, confers no credential, and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any vendor or tradition. All scenarios are original analytical exercises; no exam content is reproduced. Esoteric claims are presented as objects of study, not as established fact.

choices: That everything in the universe is literally identical
That patterns repeat across scales — microcosm and macrocosm correspond — a claim about analogy, not identity
That astrology is a proven science
That the tablet is a recipe for transmuting lead
evidence: Paraphrase of the Emerald Tablet's famous line: 'That which is above is as that which is below.' (Public-domain translations vary.)
scenarios.hint: 'As' is a simile word — what kind of claim uses similes?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most defensible reading of the correspondence claim?
scenarios.situation: A study group debates the Emerald Tablet's most famous line: 'that which is above is as that which is below.'
scenarios.title: As above, so below
scenarios.why: The careful reading is structural analogy: patterns at one scale illuminate patterns at another (microcosm/macrocosm). 'As' signals correspondence, not identity — the text doesn't claim a planet IS an atom. Collapsing analogy into identity is how careful metaphysics becomes sloppy mysticism; holding the distinction is the whole critical skill.

choices: That matter is an illusion with no properties
That mind or perception is primary in the account of reality — an idealist claim to be analyzed, not assumed
That thinking hard enough manifests wealth
That ancient authors understood neuroscience
evidence: Paraphrase of the Principle of Mentalism: 'All is Mind; the universe is mental.' (The Kybalion, 1908, anonymous 'Three Initiates' — public domain.)
scenarios.hint: Treat it as a philosophical position — which classical position does 'all is mind' resemble?
scenarios.prompt: How should a critical reader handle the Principle of Mentalism?
scenarios.situation: The Kybalion's first principle declares 'All is Mind.'
scenarios.title: The mental universe
scenarios.why: Read it as a metaphysical thesis in the idealist family (compare Berkeley): reality fundamentally mental rather than material. The critical move is neither belief nor dismissal but analysis — what would follow if it were true, what evidence could bear on it, where it begs the question. 'Manifesting wealth' is a modern prosperity-gospel retrofit, not the text's claim.

choices: As a metaphorical frame: everything is in motion and change — to be read alongside the text's worldview, not as physics
As a verified statement of quantum mechanics
As proof the authors knew about atoms
As meaningless filler
evidence: Paraphrase of the Principle of Vibration: 'Nothing rests; everything moves; everything vibrates.'
scenarios.hint: Ask what work the claim does inside the text's own system before asking whether modern physics agrees.
scenarios.prompt: What is the responsible interpretation?
scenarios.situation: 'Nothing rests; everything moves; everything vibrates.' A forum claims this anticipates quantum field theory.
scenarios.title: The vibrating universe
scenarios.why: Inside the text's worldview, the principle frames reality as process rather than static substance — a metaphysical commitment, not a lab result. Retrojecting quantum mechanics onto it is anachronism: it borrows science's prestige without its method. The honest reading asks what the claim meant to its authors and what it does in their system.

choices: The author ran out of papyrus
Aphoristic density: each line is meant to be unfolded through commentary and contemplation — the brevity is the pedagogy
It was never meant to be read
Short texts can't carry meaning
evidence: The Emerald Tablet: roughly a dozen lines total, in most translations.
scenarios.hint: What kind of teaching fits in twelve lines — information transfer, or something else?
scenarios.prompt: Why is the Emerald Tablet so short?
scenarios.situation: The most famous alchemical text in the Western tradition is barely a page long.
scenarios.title: The twelve-line classic
scenarios.why: Aphoristic form is a technology: compressed, memorable lines designed to be unfolded slowly through commentary, memorization, and meditation. The brevity isn't missing content — it's the pedagogy. This is why the Tablet generated centuries of commentaries vastly longer than itself: the form invites exegesis the way a seed invites a tree.

choices: That opposites are unrelated
That hot and cold are different substances
That opposites are poles of one continuum — temperature, not two essences — differing in degree
That logic's law of non-contradiction is false
evidence: Paraphrase of the Principle of Polarity: 'Everything has its pair of opposites; opposites are identical in nature but different in degree.'
scenarios.hint: Hot and cold: two things, or one scale with two ends?
scenarios.prompt: What does the Polarity principle actually claim?
scenarios.situation: 'Opposites are identical in nature, different in degree.'
scenarios.title: The poles of one thing
scenarios.why: The claim is that many opposites are endpoints of a single spectrum — hot/cold as temperature, light/dark as illumination. It's an observation about continua, and a decent one: pre-modern thinkers noticed what thermometers later formalized. It doesn't refute logic (a thing can't be wholly hot and wholly cold at once) — it reframes opposition as gradation.

choices: Ficino's 15th-century Latin translation made the Corpus available to Renaissance readers, who read it as ancient Egyptian wisdom — a dating later scholarship revised
Renaissance readers ignored it completely
It was written in the Renaissance
Translation never changes how a text is received
evidence: Marsilio Ficino translated the Corpus Hermeticum into Latin in the 1400s; readers took it for primordial Egyptian wisdom. Later scholarship dated the texts to the 2nd–3rd centuries CE.
scenarios.hint: What happens to a text's authority when its assumed age changes by a millennium?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the reception history matter?
scenarios.situation: Renaissance humanists treated the Corpus Hermeticum as older than Moses; modern scholarship places it in Roman Egypt.
scenarios.title: The misdated classic
scenarios.why: The texts' authority for Renaissance readers came largely from their supposed antiquity — 'prisca theologia,' ancient theology. Redating them to the 2nd–3rd centuries CE doesn't erase their interest, but it relocates it: from primordial revelation to a fascinating product of Hellenistic Egypt's religious ferment. Reception history teaches that what a text MEANT to readers is itself historical data.

scenarios.title: The 1908 Bestseller
scenarios.situation: A popular course teaches 'the seven Hermetic principles from the ancient Kybalion' as 2,000-year-old Egyptian wisdom. Students are memorizing the principles as antiquity.
evidence: Deslippe's attribution case; no pre-1908 trace; New Thought content analysis.
scenarios.prompt: What is the accurate framing?
choices: The Kybalion is a 1908 New Thought work (almost certainly William Walker Atkinson writing as 'Three Initiates') — its principles are a modern systematization, valuable as such, but not ancient Egyptian transmission. Teaching it as antiquity misdates it by two millennia; teaching it as a modern classic is accurate and still honors its influence.
It's ancient; scholars are wrong.
It's worthless because it's modern.
The dating doesn't matter.
scenarios.hint: A course teaches the Kybalion's principles as ancient Egyptian wisdom — what is the accurate framing?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the documented attribution, separates authenticity from value, and prescribes the accurate framing (modern classic, not ancient transmission). B denies evidence; C confuses dating with worth; D abandons the historical question the course itself raises.

choices: Dee channeled everything alone in trance
Kelley scryed (reported visions) while Dee meticulously recorded in diaries — the division of labor shapes what we can know
The angels wrote the diaries themselves
No records survive
evidence: 1582–1589: Edward Kelley acted as scryer, reporting visions; John Dee recorded sessions in detailed diaries.
scenarios.hint: One man saw, the other wrote — what does that division do to the evidence?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the Dee/Kelley division of labor matter for evaluating the material?
scenarios.situation: The Enochian material comes from sessions where Kelley reported visions and Dee wrote them down.
scenarios.title: The seer and the scribe
scenarios.why: Every claim passes through two filters: Kelley's perception and reporting, Dee's transcription and systematizing. Source criticism starts here — we have Dee's records of Kelley's reports, not direct access to anything else. This doesn't settle truth or fraud, but it defines exactly what the evidence IS: a meticulous secondhand record, invaluable whatever its origin.

choices: It's a naturally evolved language like English
It's a constructed script with its own alphabet, delivered as a received system — interesting precisely because of its systematicity
It's random gibberish with no structure
It's a cipher for Latin with no original content
evidence: The Enochian corpus includes a complete alphabet, vocabulary, and grammar fragments, recorded systematically across years.
scenarios.hint: Natural languages evolve messily over centuries — what does instant systematicity suggest?
scenarios.prompt: What is analytically interesting about Enochian as a language?
scenarios.situation: The Enochian corpus includes a full alphabet and consistent vocabulary delivered over several years.
scenarios.title: The received alphabet
scenarios.why: A complete, internally consistent script appearing in a few years is remarkable whether one attributes it to angels, the unconscious, or fraud — each hypothesis must explain the systematicity. Linguists note its structures; historians note the delivery method. The interesting question isn't just 'real or fake' but 'what kind of human (or other) process produces systematic novelty like this?'

choices: 48 structured invocations (Calls/Keys), each tied to parts of a cosmological system — the architecture is the point
48 random poems
A single prayer repeated
A shopping list
evidence: The 48 Calls/Keys: a fixed sequence of invocations mapped onto the system's cosmology.
scenarios.hint: Why forty-eight, in order, mapped to a cosmos — what does fixed structure enable that spontaneity doesn't?
scenarios.prompt: What makes the Calls a system rather than a collection?
scenarios.situation: The Enochian material culminates in 48 Calls/Keys in fixed sequence.
scenarios.title: The forty-eight calls
scenarios.why: Fixed sequence + cosmological mapping = a navigable architecture: each Call addresses a specific region of the system's universe, in order. That's what makes it a system — interlocking parts with defined relations — rather than inspired fragments. Whether one 'uses' it or studies it, the systematicity is the datum: somebody built (or received) a complete machine, not a pile of parts.

choices: They invented it independently
The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn (founded 1888) integrated Enochian into its curriculum — a major transmission channel to modern occultism
It was lost until the internet
Victorian scientists debunked it permanently
evidence: The Golden Dawn's papers include extensive Enochian material adapted from Dee's manuscripts.
scenarios.hint: Ideas travel through institutions — which institution carried Enochian from the 1500s to the 1900s?
scenarios.prompt: How did Enochian reach the modern era?
scenarios.situation: Dee's manuscripts sat in libraries for centuries; today Enochian is everywhere in occultism.
scenarios.title: The Victorian bridge
scenarios.why: The Golden Dawn systematized Dee's manuscripts into teachable grade material, and its members and successors carried it into 20th-century occultism. Transmission reshapes: the Golden Dawn's Enochian is Dee's material refracted through Victorian magical theory. Studying the chain of custody — manuscript to order to book to forum — is how you separate the 16th-century artifact from its later varnish.

choices: They're decorative doodles
Tables, squares, and letter-grids function as a notation: positions encode relations, like coordinates or code
They're maps of real places
Notation can't carry meaning
evidence: Enochian practice centers on lettered squares and tables — e.g., grids whose cells map to entities and regions.
scenarios.hint: A spreadsheet's meaning lives in which cell holds what — what if a magic square works the same way?
scenarios.prompt: What is the analytical payoff of reading the squares as notation?
scenarios.situation: Enochian workings revolve around lettered grids and tables.
scenarios.title: The magic spreadsheet
scenarios.why: Read as notation, the squares are data structures: cell positions encode cosmological addresses, and operations on the grid are computations over that space. This reframes 'magic squares' as information design — humanity's recurring trick of laying knowledge out in grids (compare astrological charts, periodic tables, memory palaces). The medium is part of the message.

choices: Apply source criticism: cross-check diary consistency, look for contemporary corroboration, weigh motives — the same toolkit as any historical claim
Accept or reject based on gut feeling
Declare it true because it's old
Declare it false because it's weird
evidence: Question: were Kelley's visions genuine experiences, conscious fraud, or something else?
scenarios.hint: Historians evaluate miracle claims, forgeries, and visions with the same toolkit — what is in that toolkit?
scenarios.prompt: How does a historian approach the authenticity question?
scenarios.situation: Were Kelley's visions genuine, fraudulent, or something in between?
scenarios.title: The authenticity question
scenarios.why: Same toolkit as any historical puzzle: internal consistency across years of diaries, contemporary corroboration, cui bono (who benefits), psychological plausibility, and the hard cases that resist both 'true' and 'fraud' (e.g., sincere self-deception, cryptomnesia). 'Weird, therefore false' is as lazy as 'old, therefore true.' The method doesn't guarantee an answer — it guarantees an honest one.

scenarios.title: The Call with the Wrong Table
scenarios.situation: A practitioner performs an Aethyr Call while visualizing the elemental tablets — mixing the Heptarchic and Aethyr systems. They report confusing results and blame the language.
evidence: Aethyr Call text + elemental tablet visualization mixed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the structural error?
choices: Category error: the Aethyr Calls govern the 30 visionary regions, not the elemental tablets — the Heptarchic Calls are the tablet technology. Mixing the systems' architectures produces incoherence; the 'confusing results' reflect confused method, not a defective language.
Their pronunciation was wrong.
The Calls don't work.
They need a better scryer.
scenarios.hint: An Aethyr Call performed with elemental-tablet visualization gives confusing results — why?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The Enochian system has distinct subsystems with distinct functions; the practitioner's confusion came from crossing them. The diagnosis is structural and fixable — learn the architecture. B, C, D all miss the category error.

scenarios.title: The Tablet with the Black Cross
scenarios.situation: A student's Great Table copy shows a 'black cross' variant they've seen online, presented as Dee's original. They want to know whether to use it.
evidence: no source cited; grid differs from Sloane MS in 6 squares.
scenarios.prompt: What is the critical question?
choices: Provenance: which manuscript, which edition, whose reconstruction? The tablets exist in multiple manuscript versions and modern reconstructions that differ in details — 'Dee's original' needs a specific source. Evaluate the variant by its documentation, not its internet popularity; and note that small grid differences change the angel names derived from it.
Use it; the internet is democratic.
Black crosses are more powerful.
All versions are identical.
scenarios.hint: An online 'black cross' tablet variant claims to be Dee's original — how do you evaluate it?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The tablets' manuscript tradition has real variants, and the letter-grid determines derived names — so the version matters functionally, not just scholarly. Provenance questions (which manuscript? whose edition?) are the method. B, C, D all abandon source criticism.

scenarios.title: The Diary Entry Out of Order
scenarios.situation: A popular book quotes a dramatic diary entry as the sessions' climax, but the entry is dated two years before the events the book places it among. The chronology is scrambled for narrative effect.
evidence: quoted entry dated 1583; book places it in the 1585 narrative.
scenarios.prompt: What is the critical correction?
choices: Restore the chronology: the diaries' dated sequence is the primary evidence, and rearranging it for drama misrepresents the process — the 'climax' framing is the author's narrative imposed on Dee's record. Check dramatic quotations against the dated text; the dull chronological truth outranks the exciting rearrangement.
The drama matters more than dates.
Diaries shouldn't be read chronologically.
The book's narrative is the real teaching.
scenarios.hint: A book scrambles the diaries' chronology for dramatic effect — what is lost?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The diaries' value is precisely their dated, sequential record of a process unfolding — scrambling the order destroys the evidence while keeping the excitement. The dull chronology is the data; the drama is the distortion. B, C, D all sacrifice evidence for narrative.

choices: A straight line from input to output
A loop: output is measured and fed back to adjust input — the thermostat as the canonical model
A type of computer virus
A management fad with no content
evidence: Paraphrase of Wiener (1948): control and communication in the animal and the machine, via feedback.
scenarios.hint: A thermostat doesn't just heat — it measures. What does the measurement do?
scenarios.prompt: What is a feedback loop, and why did Wiener think it mattered universally?
scenarios.situation: Wiener's 1948 'Cybernetics' claims feedback explains everything from thermostats to nervous systems.
scenarios.title: The thermostat principle
scenarios.why: Feedback: sense the output, compare to the goal, adjust the input — the loop that lets systems steer. Wiener's leap was seeing the same loop in machines, organisms, and societies: purposeful behavior without a little homunculus inside, just circular causality. Whether the universality holds is debatable; the loop itself is one of the 20th century's great ideas.

choices: It's the same as first-order cybernetics
It includes the observer in the system: the act of observing/modeling changes what's observed
It's about better thermostats
It's a refutation of Wiener
evidence: Second-order cybernetics: the observer is part of the system observed.
scenarios.hint: A thermostat doesn't know it's being studied — but what about an economist studying a market?
scenarios.prompt: What changes when the observer is inside the system?
scenarios.situation: An economist's model of a market starts moving the market.
scenarios.title: The observer effect
scenarios.why: Second-order cybernetics notes that social systems contain their own observers: predictions alter behavior (self-fulfilling or self-defeating prophecies), measurements disturb. The thermostat is first-order — observed from outside. The market is second-order — the map redraws the territory. Any social science that ignores this is doing first-order work on second-order material.

choices: Fiction that makes itself real: stories, models, or beliefs that bootstrap themselves into causal efficacy
Superstition about hype
A synonym for lying
A type of computer malware
evidence: Paraphrase of the CCRU-associated concept: hyperstition — fictions that engineer their own truth.
scenarios.hint: A rumor crashes a bank by causing a run — the rumor was false, then true. What do you call that?
scenarios.prompt: What is hyperstition, in one careful sentence?
scenarios.situation: The CCRU's signature concept needs a precise definition.
scenarios.title: Fiction that builds itself
scenarios.why: Hyperstition: a fiction that makes itself real through the feedback loops it triggers — the bank-run rumor, the self-fulfilling investment thesis, the manifesto that recruits its own movement. It's second-order cybernetics applied to narrative: stories as causal agents. The concept earns its keep wherever beliefs move markets, politics, or code — which is to say, everywhere social.

choices: A conventional academic department
A 1990s Warwick collective (Nick Land, Sadie Plant and others) blending theory, fiction, and electronic music into a deliberately destabilizing writing practice
A software company
A religious movement
evidence: The Cybernetic Culture Research Unit operated at the University of Warwick in the late 1990s.
scenarios.hint: What happens to 'research output' when the researchers treat genres as materials rather than containers?
scenarios.prompt: What was the CCRU, analytically speaking?
scenarios.situation: You need to place the CCRU for readers who've only heard the name.
scenarios.title: The Warwick experiment
scenarios.why: A philosophy collective that treated theory-fiction, jungle music, and cybernetics as one continuous practice — deliberately dissolving the line between analyzing systems and performing them. Analytically, it's a case study in method: what knowledge becomes possible when you stop respecting genre boundaries? Whether the results are genius or noise, the experiment asks a real question about how thinking happens.

choices: That time travel is physically proven
A CCRU-associated motif: time as non-linear, with the future leaking into the present — read as a theoretical fiction about feedback, not a physics claim
That clocks run backwards in Lemuria
That history has no patterns
evidence: Motif in CCRU-adjacent writing: future events causing present ones; 'the Lemurian time war.'
scenarios.hint: If hyperstition is fiction-becoming-real, what does time look like from inside that process?
scenarios.prompt: How should a critical reader handle the 'time war' material?
scenarios.situation: CCRU-adjacent texts describe futures causing presents — a 'time war.'
scenarios.title: The time war
scenarios.why: Read it as theory-fiction: a thought experiment in which hyperstitional feedback is radicalized until causality itself loops — the future 'causing' the present the way a rumor causes the run. It's not physics; it's what happens when you push 'beliefs are causal' to its limit as a literary-philosophical device. The critical reader asks what the fiction illuminates (reflexivity, anticipation) without mistaking the device for a discovery.

choices: Treat unfalsifiability as a warning: if no possible evidence could dent the framework, it's a lens, not a finding — useful for generating readings, not for settling questions
Accept every hyperstitional claim as true
Dismiss the whole thing as nonsense
Use it to predict stock prices
evidence: Claim: 'This text is hyperstitionally engineering its own reception.'
scenarios.hint: What test could prove that claim wrong? If none exists, what kind of claim is it?
scenarios.prompt: Where does the hyperstition framework overreach?
scenarios.situation: A text claims to be hyperstitionally engineering its own reception — conveniently immune to criticism.
scenarios.title: The unfalsifiable loop
scenarios.why: When a framework explains away all counter-evidence ('your skepticism is part of the loop'), it's stopped being a hypothesis and become a lens: productive for generating readings, useless for adjudicating truth. The honest use of hyperstition marks this boundary explicitly. Frameworks that can't lose can't win either — they can only redescribe.

scenarios.title: The Model That Models the Modeler
scenarios.situation: A team builds a 'developer productivity' dashboard measuring commits and PRs. Within months, developers optimize for the metrics — smaller PRs, more commits — and the dashboard now measures its own effects. Leadership treats the numbers as objective productivity data.
evidence: commits +40%, PR size -60%, 'productivity' up; developers report metric-optimizing.
scenarios.prompt: What is the second-order analysis?
choices: The dashboard is inside the system it measures: Goodhart's law is a second-order phenomenon — the observer's distinctions (what counts as 'productive') reshaped the observed behavior, and the numbers now report the measurement's effects, not the underlying reality. Treating them as objective repeats the first-order error.
The metrics are wrong; find better ones.
Developers are gaming the system; punish them.
Dashboards don't work.
scenarios.hint: A productivity dashboard now measures its own effects — what is the analysis?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It identifies the reflexivity (measurement changing the measured) and names the error (first-order objectivity claimed for second-order data). Better metrics (B) would be gamed in turn; punishment (C) misses the structural point; (D) abandons measurement instead of understanding it.

scenarios.title: The Idea That Replicated
scenarios.situation: A baseless rumor about a product defect spreads across social media in hours, tanks the stock 8%, and triggers a recall investigation — all before anyone verifies the claim. The rumor was engineered: short, alarming, shareable.
scenarios.prompt: What does the meme's-eye view reveal?
choices: The rumor was optimized for fitness, not truth: high fecundity (alarming + shareable), adequate fidelity (the core claim survives retelling), and the market's reaction (the stock drop) then becomes 'evidence' for the rumor — a hyperstitional loop where replication manufactures its own confirmation.
The market is irrational.
Someone should have fact-checked faster.
Rumors are harmless.
scenarios.hint: An engineered rumor tanks a stock before verification — what is the memetic analysis?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It analyzes the rumor as a replicator (fitness components identified) and spots the hyperstitional loop — the consequences of belief becoming evidence for the belief. B moralizes; C is true but misses the mechanism; D is refuted by the 8% drop.

scenarios.title: The Manifesto with No Author
scenarios.situation: An anonymous text circulates calling to 'accelerate the process' — readers variously take it as leftist liberation politics, techno-capitalist cheerleading, and artistic provocation. Factions argue over its 'true meaning.'
evidence: three factions, three incompatible readings, one shared word.
scenarios.prompt: What does the contested-signifier analysis say?
choices: The text's meaning is underdetermined by design (or by the term's history) — 'accelerationism' now names at least three incompatible projects, so the factions are arguing past each other using the same word. The productive move is mapping: which mutation does each reading invoke, and what does each faction want the term to do?
Find the author; they'll settle it.
The leftist reading is correct.
Burn it.
scenarios.hint: Factions fight over an anonymous 'accelerationist' text's true meaning — what is the analysis?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It applies the domain's central analytical move — disambiguate the contested signifier, map the mutations, ask what work the term does — instead of joining the faction fight. B seeks an authority the text's history won't supply; C picks a team; D is anti-intellectual.

choices: Words naturally resemble what they mean
The link between signifier (sound/image) and signified (concept) is arbitrary — 'tree' could have been any sound
All languages share one vocabulary
Meaning lives in dictionaries
evidence: Paraphrase: the linguistic sign unites a sound-image and a concept; their bond is arbitrary.
scenarios.hint: Is there anything tree-like about the sounds t-r-ee? Check another language's word for it.
scenarios.prompt: What does Saussure's arbitrariness claim mean?
scenarios.situation: Why is a tree called 'tree'?
scenarios.title: Why 'tree'
scenarios.why: Nothing about t-r-ee resembles a tree — Spanish says árbol, Japanese says ki. The sign works by social convention, not natural resemblance. This arbitrariness is what makes language flexible (any meaning can attach to any sound) and what makes translation lossy (conventions differ). Every symbol system — including code — inherits this: variable names mean by agreement.

choices: It made writing prettier
It democratized literacy: a small set of reusable signs (20-odd letters) can encode any utterance, versus thousands of memorized glyphs
It was invented for magic
It had no cognitive effects
evidence: Alphabetic scripts use ~20-40 signs; logographic systems need thousands.
scenarios.hint: Compare the learning curve: memorizing 26 shapes versus 3000 — who gets to read?
scenarios.prompt: What did the alphabet do to thought?
scenarios.situation: The alphabet replaced systems needing thousands of memorized signs.
scenarios.title: The 26-shape revolution
scenarios.why: A tiny reusable sign-set collapses the cost of literacy: anyone can learn 26 shapes, so reading stops being a scribal monopoly. The cognitive effects run deep — alphabetic literacy trains sequential, analytic processing (some argue at the expense of holistic modes). Technologies of notation aren't neutral containers; they rewire what their users can think. Code editors are the latest chapter.

choices: Supernatural entities read them
Psychologically: condensing an intention into a symbol gives the mind a handle — focus, commitment, and pattern-noticing do the work, no spirits required
They rewrite physics
They work by placebo alone, which means not at all
evidence: Sigil practice: write an intention, reduce it to an abstract glyph, then 'charge' it through focus.
scenarios.hint: Separate the mechanism from the metaphysics — what does the procedure do to attention?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most defensible account of why sigils 'work' for practitioners?
scenarios.situation: Practitioners report sigils effective; you need a non-supernatural analysis.
scenarios.title: The condensed intention
scenarios.why: The procedure is attention technology: articulating a goal precisely, compressing it into a memorable glyph, then focusing intensely. That combination — clarity plus commitment plus heightened pattern-noticing afterward — plausibly changes behavior, which changes outcomes. You don't need spirits to explain why writing down goals works; psychologists have the receipts. The symbol is an interface to the practitioner's own cognition.

choices: Notation is just shorthand with no cognitive role
Mathematical notation is a symbol system that extends thought: it makes complex relations manipulable — you can literally calculate with the symbols
Only geniuses benefit from notation
Notation and language are unrelated
evidence: Example: Leibniz's dy/dx notation invites treating derivatives as fractions — sometimes fruitfully.
scenarios.hint: Try doing long division with Roman numerals — what does the notation let your hands do that your head can't?
scenarios.prompt: What does mathematical notation do, analytically?
scenarios.situation: Why did better notation accelerate mathematics historically?
scenarios.title: Thinking with symbols
scenarios.why: Notation externalizes cognition: positional numerals, algebraic symbols, and dy/dx turn mental operations into visual manipulations you can perform reliably. Leibniz's notation even suggests true theorems by analogy. Symbol systems aren't just records of thought — they're scaffolding that lets thought climb higher. Programming languages are this principle industrialized.

choices: Emoji are a regression to illiteracy
Emoji function like rebus writing: pictographs carrying flexible, context-dependent meaning — a new layer on alphabetic text, not a replacement
Emoji have fixed dictionary meanings
Images can't be language
evidence: Texts studded with emoji: the pictures modify tone and meaning of the words.
scenarios.hint: Do emoji replace the words, or do something to the words?
scenarios.prompt: What are emoji, linguistically?
scenarios.situation: Emoji saturate digital writing; linguists are paying attention.
scenarios.title: The rebus returns
scenarios.why: Emoji work like rebus pictographs: context-flexible symbols that modulate alphabetic text — marking tone, softening requests, disambiguating intent. They're not replacing the alphabet but adding a paralinguistic layer (the digital equivalent of facial expression). Symbol systems evolve: five thousand years after pictographs, we've reinvented them for the medium that needed them.

choices: Variable names are sigils-by-agreement: condensed symbols the team charges with shared meaning through use
Code has no symbolic dimension
Naming doesn't matter
Only the compiler's reading counts
evidence: A codebase where 'phoenix' means the retry subsystem — to insiders, the word hums with meaning.
scenarios.hint: What does 'phoenix' mean to the compiler versus to the team?
scenarios.prompt: What is the symbolic dimension of code?
scenarios.situation: The team's codebase is full of names that carry lore: 'phoenix,' 'the pit,' 'grandma's cache.'
scenarios.title: The codebase as grimoire
scenarios.why: To the compiler, names are arbitrary tokens (Saussure would nod); to the team, they're condensed shared meaning — sigils by agreement. Good names charge a symbol with intent so future readers grasp purpose instantly; bad names are dead glyphs. This is why naming is the hardest problem: you're minting currency for a symbol economy.

scenarios.title: The Bindrune with No Source
scenarios.situation: A popular 'Viking bindrune' for protection circulates online — combining runes in an arrangement with no historical precedent, presented as ancient Norse magic. Thousands have tattooed it.
evidence: no pre-2000 source for this arrangement; revival-lineage design.
scenarios.prompt: What is the critical assessment?
choices: It's a modern creation wearing antiquity's clothes: bindrunes existed (ligatures in inscriptions), but this specific arrangement has no historical source — it's contemporary design, probably via the 20th-century revival lineage. As modern art it's fine; as 'ancient Norse magic' it's mislabeled. The tattoos are real commitments to a fiction — assess the design's aesthetics separately from its historical claims.
It's ancient; the internet preserves tradition.
All bindrunes are fake.
Tattoos are always mistakes.
scenarios.hint: A viral 'ancient Viking bindrune' has no historical source — what is the assessment?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It distinguishes the general practice (bindrunes attested) from the specific artifact (this arrangement, unsourced), separates aesthetic from historical judgment, and notes the real stakes (permanent body art based on false history). B is credulous; C overcorrects; D is irrelevant moralizing.

scenarios.title: The Chart with the Wrong Houses
scenarios.situation: A student's astrology software defaults to Placidus houses; their textbook teaches whole-sign. Their chart readings contradict themselves — the same planet 'in the 10th' (Placidus) versus 'in the 9th' (whole-sign), with different interpretations each way.
scenarios.prompt: What is the methodological fix?
choices: Pick one house system and use it consistently — the contradiction comes from mixing systems, not from the chart. Learn the chosen system's logic, note that the other exists, and never blend their placements. (Which system is 'correct' is a separate, genuinely debated question.)
Average the two placements.
The software is wrong.
Houses don't matter.
scenarios.hint: Mixed house systems give contradictory placements — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The error is methodological (system-mixing), not substantive — each house system is internally coherent, and blending them produces the contradictions. The parenthetical honestly notes the genuine debate without requiring its resolution for consistent practice. B is nonsense; C picks a team arbitrarily; D abandons the grammar.

scenarios.title: The Pentagram That Wasn't
scenarios.situation: A viral image shows a 'perfect pentagram' in a flower, a galaxy, and a corporate logo — 'proof of the universe's hidden geometry.' Measurement shows: the flower approximates it, the galaxy is a spiral (not a pentagram), the logo was designed that way.
evidence: flower: approximate 5-fold; galaxy: spiral; logo: designed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the assessment?
choices: Mixed: the flower's approximate pentagram is genuine morphology (phyllotaxis does produce fivefold patterns); the galaxy is misidentified (spiral ≠ pentagram); the logo is intentional design, not discovery. Lumping them as one 'proof' is pareidolia-plus-marketing — each claim needs its own measurement, and 'hidden geometry' explains nothing until specified.
It's all proof of sacred geometry.
It's all coincidence.
Geometry is meaningless.
scenarios.hint: A viral image claims pentagrams in a flower, a galaxy, and a logo — what is the measured assessment?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It evaluates each claim separately — genuine morphology, misidentification, intentional design — instead of accepting or rejecting the bundle. The closing methodological point (specify the claim, measure it) is the portable discipline. B is credulous; C overcorrects; D is nihilism.

choices: Apply today's definitions; words mean what they mean now
Recover the author's context first: what did key terms mean then, to whom, against what debates?
Assume all old texts agree with each other
Skip context; the text speaks for itself
evidence: A 17th-century text praises 'enthusiasm' — then a positive term for divine inspiration.
scenarios.hint: 'Enthusiasm' is now an insult-adjacent word for overexcitement — what breaks if you import that?
scenarios.prompt: How do you avoid misreading it?
scenarios.situation: A 17th-century text praises 'enthusiasm' — but the word's meaning has inverted since.
scenarios.title: The shifting word
scenarios.why: Recover period meaning first: 'enthusiasm' then meant divine inspiration, not naive overexcitement. Reading with modern definitions manufactures nonsense the author never wrote. Historical semantics is the entry fee for old texts — check the OED's dated senses, read contemporaries, and never trust a familiar word.

choices: Pick the translation that sounds best
Compare translations, check key terms against the original language, and note where translators disagree — the disagreements are data
Translations are all equivalent
Learn every ancient language first or don't read
evidence: Three translations of one passage render a key term as 'mind,' 'spirit,' and 'breath.'
scenarios.hint: Mind, spirit, breath — one source word, three Englishes. What does the spread tell you?
scenarios.prompt: How do you read across translations responsibly?
scenarios.situation: One key term appears as 'mind,' 'spirit,' and 'breath' in three translations.
scenarios.title: The three translations
scenarios.why: The spread marks a concept English splits three ways — the original likely means something like 'animating principle' covering all three. Compare translations, consult the source term, and treat translator disagreement as information about conceptual mismatch, not noise. Monolingual reading of translated esoterica is reading one person's interpretation as the text.

choices: Take everything literally; symbols are for the weak
Determine the genre first: cosmology, allegory, ritual manual, and polemic each demand different reading stances
Literal is always safer
Symbolic is always deeper
evidence: A text describes the soul's ascent through seven planetary spheres.
scenarios.hint: Is this a travel itinerary, a meditation manual, or a cosmological claim — and how would you tell?
scenarios.prompt: Literal ascent or symbolic map?
scenarios.situation: A text describes the soul ascending through seven planetary spheres.
scenarios.title: The seven spheres
scenarios.why: Genre decides the reading stance: a ritual manual's ascent is a visualization protocol; a cosmology's is a truth claim; an allegory's is a moral map. Clues live in surrounding instructions ('visualize,' 'contemplate'), contemporary parallels, and the text's own signals. Defaulting to literal (or to 'everything is symbolic') without genre evidence is how both fundamentalism and mushy perennialism are born.

choices: The text's claims about itself
Who wrote it, for whom, in what circumstances, and to what end — then read the text against those interests
The prettiest interpretation
What modern readers wish it said
evidence: An anonymous 1908 text claims ancient Egyptian lineage for its teachings.
scenarios.hint: 1908, anonymous, claims Egypt — what does each of those facts suggest you check?
scenarios.prompt: How do you evaluate the lineage claim?
scenarios.situation: An anonymous 1908 text claims its teachings descend from ancient Egypt.
scenarios.title: The Egyptian lineage
scenarios.why: Ask who benefits: anonymity shields authors from scrutiny; antiquity borrows authority; 1908 situates it in the occult revival's market for ancient wisdom. Then check: do the 'Egyptian' teachings match what Egyptology knows of Egypt, or what 1908 occultists imagined? Source criticism doesn't disprove the teachings' value — it correctly prices the lineage claim.

choices: Ignore it; old texts can't contain new ideas
Flag it: ideas or terms that postdate the text's composition signal later interpolation, forgery, or misdating
Celebrate it as proof of ancient genius
Anachronisms don't matter
evidence: A '15th-century' manuscript discusses concepts from 19th-century psychology.
scenarios.hint: A text can't quote the future — so what are the live hypotheses when it seems to?
scenarios.prompt: What do you do with the time-traveling concept?
scenarios.situation: A supposedly 15th-century manuscript uses 19th-century psychological concepts.
scenarios.title: The time-traveling term
scenarios.why: Anachronism is evidence: the live hypotheses are later interpolation, misdating, or forgery (or a genuinely independent anticipation — rare, and needing strong proof). Dating by ideas is standard philology. Note the asymmetry: one solid anachronism can sink a dating claim, while absence of anachronisms only fails to sink it.

choices: Weave them into one timeless 'esoteric teaching,' smoothing contradictions
Keep sources distinct: map each claim to its source, note agreements and tensions, and let contradictions stand as data
Pick your favorite source and ignore the rest
Contradictions mean it's all false
evidence: Three traditions describe 'the subtle body' in mutually incompatible ways.
scenarios.hint: What do you lose when you iron out the contradictions — and who benefits from the ironing?
scenarios.prompt: How do you synthesize without conflating?
scenarios.situation: Three traditions describe the subtle body incompatibly.
scenarios.title: The three bodies
scenarios.why: Map claims to sources, preserve tensions, and ask why each tradition shaped the concept its way — the contradictions are data about different practices and metaphysics, not noise to smooth. Perennialist blending manufactures a 'timeless teaching' none of the sources actually taught. Honest synthesis compares; it doesn't puree.

scenarios.title: The Manuscript with Two Hands
scenarios.situation: A manuscript's main text is in a 14th-century hand, but three chapters are in a 16th-century hand on different parchment, with terminology the earlier chapters don't use. The catalog lists it as a 14th-century work.
evidence: hand A 14th c., hand B 16th c.; parchment differs; terminology differs.
scenarios.prompt: What does codicology conclude?
choices: Composite manuscript: the core is 14th-century, three chapters are 16th-century additions on different parchment — the catalog's single date is wrong, and the added chapters must be dated (and evaluated) separately. Different hands, different parchment, different terminology: three independent tests converging on composite production.
It's all 14th century; hands vary.
The 16th-century chapters are forgeries.
Parchment doesn't matter.
scenarios.hint: One manuscript, two hands, two centuries — what is the codicological verdict?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It applies triangulation (hand, parchment, terminology converging) and draws the precise conclusion — composite, not forged — with the consequence (date and evaluate separately). B ignores the evidence; C moralizes; D dismisses a whole evidence class.

scenarios.title: The Term That Changed Meaning Twice
scenarios.situation: A student builds an elaborate theory on the English word 'influence' in a translated Hermetic text — its modern sense of 'personal impact.' But the Latin 'influentia' meant stellar emanation (in-flowing from the stars), and the Greek behind it meant something else again.
scenarios.prompt: What is the methodological error?
choices: Reading the modern English sense back through the chain: 'influence' in the translation carries the Latin influentia (stellar in-flow), not the modern 'personal impact' — the student's theory is built on a semantic shift they didn't check. Trace terms back before theorizing on them.
The translation is bad.
The student is creative; that's fine.
Words don't matter.
scenarios.hint: A theory built on the modern sense of 'influence' in a translated text — what went wrong?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It identifies the exact failure (modern-sense projection through two semantic shifts) and the remedy (term-tracing before theorizing). The student's creativity isn't the issue — the unchecked chain is. B blames the translator for the reader's error; C and D abandon philology.

scenarios.title: The Too-Perfect Grimoire
scenarios.situation: A 'newly discovered' 16th-century grimoire appears: perfect condition, complete system, no textual problems, 'translated' by its discoverer (who sells initiations into its system). No provenance beyond the discoverer's story. Scholars note its categories match 1990s chaos magic, not 16th-century thought.
evidence: anachronistic categories; story provenance; seller benefits; perfect condition.
scenarios.prompt: What is the assessment?
choices: Probable modern production: the anachronistic categories (1990s concepts in 16th-century dress), the story-not-trail provenance, the too-perfect condition, and the cui bono (initiation sales) converge — four independent tools pointing the same way. 'Newly discovered complete ancient systems' from interested discoverers are the classic forgery profile.
It's genuine; scholars are jealous.
Condition doesn't matter.
Chaos magic is 16th century.
scenarios.hint: A 'discovered' grimoire with 1990s categories, no provenance, sold initiations — what is the verdict?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It runs the full toolkit and notes the convergence — the assessment's strength is the independence of the four signals. The profile match (complete system, interested discoverer, story provenance) is stated as pattern recognition, not proof, with the burden correctly placed. B, C, D each dismiss one evidence class.

choices: It's a practical language for production
Its 8 commands (><+-.,[]) prove computation needs almost nothing — a Turing tarpit, minimalism as a theorem about universality
It's too hard to be interesting
Minimalism has no theoretical content
scenarios.hint: If 8 commands suffice for all computation, what does that say about the other 99% of language features?
scenarios.prompt: What does Brainfuck demonstrate?
scenarios.situation: A language with 8 commands can compute anything computable.
scenarios.title: The eight-command universe
scenarios.why: Turing-completeness from ><+-.,[] shows universality needs almost nothing — loops, a pointer, increment/decrement, I/O. Everything else in programming languages is human-factors engineering: readability, safety, speed of thought. Esolangs are philosophy of computation by construction: Brainfuck asks 'what's essential?' and answers with a dare.

choices: It's just Brainfuck with different symbols
Control flow becomes geometry: the instruction pointer moves on a 2D grid, redirected by arrow commands — programs are mazes
2D is a gimmick with no semantic content
Grids can't express loops
evidence: Befunge (Chris Pressey): code on a 2D grid; > < ^ v redirect the instruction pointer.
scenarios.hint: In normal code, 'what runs next' is the next line — what if 'next' could be up?
scenarios.prompt: What is semantically novel about Befunge?
scenarios.situation: Befunge lays code on a two-dimensional grid.
scenarios.title: The maze program
scenarios.why: The program counter gains a direction on a plane: > sends it right, v down, and control flow becomes literal geometry — loops are circuits, branches are forks in a maze. It exposes how much ordinary programming leans on the hidden convention 'next = down one line.' Befunge makes sequence spatial, and in doing so reveals sequence was always a choice.

choices: It's a failed product
Parody as critique: INTERCAL's 'features' (politeness modifiers, line-noise operators) satirize real language design tics by exaggeration
Parody has no analytical value
It's meant for serious use
evidence: INTERCAL (1972): PLEASE modifiers, COME FROM statements (goto in reverse).
scenarios.hint: Satire works by exaggeration — what real tendencies is INTERCAL exaggerating?
scenarios.prompt: What does INTERCAL's parody reveal?
scenarios.situation: INTERCAL (1972) parodies programming language design: PLEASE for politeness, COME FROM as reverse-goto.
scenarios.title: The parody compiler
scenarios.why: COME FROM inverts goto and thereby indicts it — showing unstructured jumps are absurd from either direction. PLEASE satirizes arbitrary compiler strictness. Parody is analysis by caricature: by pushing design tics past the line, INTERCAL maps exactly where the line is. The joke only lands if you know the real languages — which is the point.

choices: It's a toy with nothing to say
Variables are characters, values are insults or praise: the language forces you to see naming as casting — what you call things shapes the drama of the code
Shakespeare is irrelevant to computation
Literary allusion has no place in code
evidence: Shakespeare Programming Language: variables are characters ('Romeo', 'Juliet'); assignment is dialogue.
scenarios.hint: If declaring a variable is introducing a character, what is the program?
scenarios.prompt: What does SPL reveal about naming?
scenarios.situation: In the Shakespeare Programming Language, variables are characters who speak their values to each other.
scenarios.title: The dramatis personae
scenarios.why: SPL literalizes what good programmers know: naming is casting. 'Romeo' carrying a value through scenes makes vividly clear that identifiers are roles in a drama of state — the program is a play, execution a performance. The esolang's joke is a genuine insight: code is read by humans performing it in their heads, and names are the cast list.

choices: Rituals are superstition; code is logic; no comparison
Both are precise utterances where exact repetition matters: a mispronounced word or mistyped character breaks the operation — the comparison illuminates why both traditions obsess over form
Code is magic, literally
Rituals never require precision
evidence: A ritual manual: 'speak these words exactly.' A compiler: 'syntax error on line 12.'
scenarios.hint: What happens in each tradition when you get one symbol wrong?
scenarios.prompt: What is the legitimate comparison between ritual and code?
scenarios.situation: Ritual manuals and compilers both demand exactness.
scenarios.title: The exact utterance
scenarios.why: The comparison is structural, not supernatural: both are formal systems where form carries the force — one symbol off and the rite (or program) fails. That shared exactness explains the shared psychology: practitioners of both develop reverence for precise form, version control of liturgies, and debugging of ceremonies. The analyst's move is to note the isomorphism without claiming identity — code isn't magic, but it rhymes.

choices: Constraints only limit; creativity needs total freedom
Constraints as engines: Oulipo-style rules and esolang restrictions force invention — the limitation is the technique
Esolangs are just jokes
Real artists never use constraints
evidence: Oulipo: novels without the letter 'e'; esolangs: computation without variables, without loops...
scenarios.hint: Why would anyone write a novel without 'e' — what does the missing letter produce?
scenarios.prompt: What do esolangs share with Oulipo?
scenarios.situation: Writers ban letters; programmers ban features. Both call it art.
scenarios.title: The productive ban
scenarios.why: A constraint converts an infinite, paralyzing space into a finite, explorable one — and the workarounds become the style. Perec's e-less novel and Brainfuck's variable-less tape — each forces the practitioner to route around the ban, and the routing IS the art. Constraint isn't the enemy of creativity; it's the instrument. Every esolang is an Oulipo exercise in silicon.

scenarios.title: The PLEASE That Wasn't Polite Enough
scenarios.situation: A student's INTERCAL program is rejected: 'insufficiently polite.' They added PLEASE to every line and it's now rejected for 'groveling.' They're frustrated — 'this language is broken.'
evidence: 'insufficiently polite' then 'groveling' on the same program.
scenarios.prompt: What does the parody teach?
choices: The politeness compiler rules are the lesson: INTERCAL parodies the ceremonial overhead of 1970s languages by making politeness literal and compilable — the 'right amount' of PLEASE is a joke about the 'right amount' of boilerplate. The frustration is the intended experience; the language is a critique you compile.
The compiler is buggy.
Politeness doesn't matter.
Use a real language.
scenarios.hint: INTERCAL rejects a program for insufficient, then excessive, politeness — what is the parody's point?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It reads the mechanic as the message — the parody's target (language ceremony) embodied in compilable rules — and reframes the frustration as the designed experience. B misses the genre entirely; C and D refuse the parody's terms.

scenarios.title: The HAI Without KTHXBYE
scenarios.situation: A student's LOLCODE program won't run. The code looks right — variables, loop, logic all correct — but the interpreter complains. They've been debugging the logic for an hour.
evidence: logic correct; HAI present; KTHXBYE missing.
scenarios.prompt: What is the likely problem?
choices: The program structure, not the logic: LOLCODE requires HAI to open and KTHXBYE to close — the meme-syntax includes meme-structure, and the missing closer is the classic beginner error. An hour of logic-debugging missed it because the student was reading for algorithmic errors in a language whose errors are ceremonial.
The logic is wrong.
The interpreter is broken.
Memes can't be programming.
scenarios.hint: Correct logic, broken LOLCODE program, hour of debugging — what was missed?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It diagnoses the error class (ceremonial/structural vs algorithmic) and explains why the debugging failed — the student applied the wrong error model. The lesson generalizes: know what kind of errors your language produces. B, C, D all misdiagnose.

scenarios.title: The Codel That Changed Color
scenarios.situation: An artist's Piet program worked as an image but fails as a program — one codel block's color drifted (JPEG compression shifted the hue), so the transition now encodes the wrong command. The painting still looks fine.
evidence: hue drifted 12 degrees in one block; transition table now yields wrong opcode.
scenarios.prompt: What does this reveal about the medium?
choices: Piet's dual nature as constraint: the program's correctness depends on exact colors — lossy formats corrupt the code while preserving the art. The medium demands lossless formats (PNG/BMP) and color-exact tools; the bug is a category lesson — in Piet, aesthetics and semantics are the same material, so medium choices are language choices.
The interpreter is too picky.
Art shouldn't be code.
JPEG is fine for everything.
scenarios.hint: JPEG compression broke a Piet program but not its looks — what does this teach?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It extracts the medium's essential lesson — in Piet, color IS syntax, so format choices are semantic choices — and prescribes the practice (lossless formats). The bug teaches the language's nature better than any manual. B, C, D all refuse the medium's terms.
