domains.name: The Alchemical Tradition
domains.description: From Alexandrian workshops to Newton's manuscripts: the history, practitioners, and method of alchemy.

scenarios.title: The Apparatus in the Vision
scenarios.situation: A student reads Zosimos's vision of the priest boiled in the cauldron and concludes it describes an actual human sacrifice performed by Alexandrian alchemists. They cite the vivid physical detail as evidence.
evidence: the vision appears amid apparatus descriptions; Byzantine copies frame it as allegory.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this reading?
choices: Nothing — the detail proves it happened.

It mistakes symbolic exegesis for reportage: the boiling priest is the metal suffering transformation, read through the double vision (outer process mirrors inner change) that structures all of Zosimos — the apparatus descriptions elsewhere in his work are the technical writing; the visions are the interpretive layer.
Visions have no meaning; skip them.
Zosimos never wrote visions.
scenarios.hint: Vivid detail in Zosimos's boiling-priest vision — does it describe a real sacrifice?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Zosimos writes on two registers — technical apparatus descriptions and visionary exegesis — and the tradition reads the visions as symbolic interpretations of the same processes the technical passages describe literally. A collapses the registers; C discards half the corpus; D denies the manuscript evidence.

scenarios.title: Whose Corpus Is It?
scenarios.situation: A new translation markets itself as 'the authentic 8th-century writings of Jabir ibn Hayyan.' But the texts reference authors who lived in the 10th century, use terminology that developed later, and show at least three distinct doctrinal positions on the sulfur-mercury theory.
evidence: citations postdate Jabir by 200 years; three incompatible sulfur-mercury doctrines.
scenarios.prompt: What does critical reading conclude?
choices: The attribution is traditional, not historical: internal evidence (anachronisms, multiple voices) indicates centuries of accretion under one prestigious name — the 'Jabir problem.' Treat it as a corpus, not an author.
Jabir was simply ahead of his time.
The anachronisms prove the texts are worthless.
One author, three moods.
scenarios.hint: Texts 'by Jabir' cite 10th-century authors — what does that establish?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Anachronistic references are dating evidence, not mysteries — the corpus grew over centuries with contributions attributed to the founding name, a standard pseudepigraphic pattern. B explains away evidence; C confuses authorship with value (the corpus remains enormously influential regardless); D is special pleading.

scenarios.title: Burning the Textbooks
scenarios.situation: A student admires Paracelsus's public burning of medical authorities as 'sticking it to the establishment' and concludes all established knowledge should be rejected in favor of direct experience. They cite Paracelsus as their model.
evidence: Paracelsus was university-trained; his works cite authorities extensively even while attacking them.
scenarios.prompt: What did Paracelsus actually argue?
choices: That authority must yield to evidence — he replaced textual authority with his own systematic observation and chemical medicine, not with the rejection of all knowledge. The burning was a claim about method (experience over citation), not an excuse for ignorance.
That all books should be burned.
That experience means never studying.
That the establishment is always wrong.
scenarios.hint: Paracelsus burned the textbooks — was his point 'reject all knowledge'?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Paracelsus's anti-authoritarianism was methodological: he demanded that claims answer to laboratory and bedside experience rather than to Galen's text. He was enormously learned himself — the burning was theater in service of an epistemological argument, not a rejection of learning. B, C, D mistake the theater for the thesis.

scenarios.title: The Rationalist and the Alchemist
scenarios.situation: A popular article claims Newton kept his alchemy secret because he knew it was irrational nonsense — 'even he was embarrassed.' The article cites no manuscripts.
objectives: Read the archive, not the legend
evidence: 1M+ words of systematic alchemical notebooks; Keynes's 1936 papers first revealed the scale.
scenarios.prompt: What does the archive actually show?
choices: Decades of systematic laboratory work, careful notebooks, and theoretical development — pursued with the same rigor as his physics, and continuous with his quest for nature's active principles. The secrecy reflects the era's religious and political dangers (and alchemy's legal ambiguity), not embarrassment — and the article's lack of manuscript citation is the tell.
That he was embarrassed — secrecy proves shame.
That the manuscripts are forgeries.
That Newton had a split personality.
scenarios.hint: Was Newton's alchemical secrecy proof of embarrassment?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The archive contradicts the embarrassment narrative on every point: the work is systematic, sustained, and intellectually continuous with the physics. Early modern England gave plenty of reasons for discretion (unorthodox theology was dangerous; alchemy skirted the law). B reads motive into silence; C denies the archive; D pathologizes instead of historicizing.

scenarios.title: One Cycle and Done
scenarios.situation: A practitioner performs a single dissolution-and-coagulation, declares the work complete, and is disappointed by the crude result. They conclude the method doesn't work.
evidence: the treatises prescribe repeated cycles; 'multiplication' is iteration formalized.
scenarios.prompt: What did they misunderstand?
choices: That solve et coagula is iterative — one cycle purifies partially; exaltation comes from repeated cycles, each building on the last. The texts are explicit: repetition is the method, not a sign of failure.
Nothing — one cycle should suffice.
The method requires rarer materials.
They dissolved wrong.
scenarios.hint: One solve-coagula cycle, crude result — is the method broken?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The alchemical texts insist on iteration — the same operation repeated, each cycle refining further. Expecting completion in one pass misunderstands the method's structure; it's deliberate practice, not a single trick. B denies the textual evidence; C and D look for external causes of an internal misunderstanding.

scenarios.title: The Aquinas Treatise
scenarios.situation: A manuscript titled 'Aurora Consurgens, by Thomas Aquinas' surfaces. Aquinas (1225–1274) is not known as an alchemist; the text's terminology matches 15th-century usage, and it cites authors Aquinas couldn't have read.
evidence: terminology 15th c.; cites 14th-c. authors; Aquinas d. 1274.
scenarios.prompt: What is the critical verdict?
choices: Pseudepigraphic: the internal evidence (terminology, citations) postdates Aquinas by two centuries — the attribution borrows his authority for an alchemical text, a standard practice, not a historical record of his authorship.
Aquinas wrote it secretly.
The terminology dating must be wrong.
It's worthless because the author lied.
scenarios.hint: An 'Aquinas' alchemical text uses 15th-century terms — what follows?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Two independent dating tools (terminology, citations) converge two centuries after Aquinas — the attribution is traditional/borrowed authority, not evidence. B explains away the evidence; C rejects the method to save the attribution; D confuses authorship with value.

domains.name: Kabbalah
domains.description: The Tree of Life, the sephiroth, gematria, and the Western Hermetic adaptation — Kabbalah as a system of knowledge.

scenarios.title: The Diagram with Eleven Circles
scenarios.situation: A popular book's Tree of Life diagram shows eleven circles — the author has added Da'ath (Knowledge) as a full sephirah alongside the ten, and the pillars don't balance. A student asks whether this is an advanced teaching.
evidence: 11 solid circles; pillars unbalanced; no mention of Da'ath's special status.
scenarios.prompt: What is the critical assessment?
choices: Da'ath is not an eleventh sephirah in the classical scheme — it's the 'invisible' point of union (often shown dashed or omitted), and adding it as a full circle breaks the pillar symmetry the diagram is built on. The book is either innovating without saying so or mistaken — either way, learn the classical ten first, then evaluate variations knowingly.
Eleven is the advanced version; learn it.
The number of circles doesn't matter.
Da'ath replaces Kether.
scenarios.hint: A Tree diagram shows eleven full sephiroth — is this advanced teaching?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The classical Tree has ten sephiroth; Da'ath (when shown) marks the abyss-crossing as a non-sephirah — its 'invisibility' is doctrinally significant. An eleven-circle diagram without explanation signals either unmarked innovation or error. B inverts the pedagogy; C ignores structure; D confuses the crown with the abyss.

scenarios.title: Whose Table Is It?
scenarios.situation: Two books give different Tarot-to-path attributions: one puts The Fool on path 11 (Aleph), the other on a different path entirely. A student assumes one book is simply wrong.
evidence: Book A: GD attributions; Book B: pre-GD continental arrangement.
scenarios.prompt: What is the more accurate assessment?
choices: Correspondence tables are school-specific syntheses — the Golden Dawn's attributions (Fool/Aleph on the 11th path) are one influential arrangement, not a universal fact. The books represent different lineages; the student should learn one system coherently, note the other's existence, and never mix tables unknowingly.
The older book is right.
The more expensive book is right.
Correspondences are arbitrary anyway.
scenarios.hint: Two books disagree on path attributions — is one simply wrong?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Esoteric correspondences stabilized differently in different schools and eras — 'the' table is always somebody's table. Mixing attributions from different systems produces incoherence, which is why lineage-awareness matters more than picking the 'right' one. B and C outsource judgment; D dismisses the system's internal logic.

scenarios.title: The License Plate Revelation
scenarios.situation: Someone computes English A=1/Z=26 values for their license plate, gets 666, and concludes cosmic significance. They call it gematria.
evidence: English ordinal, no tradition, no context, single match celebrated.
scenarios.prompt: What is the critical response?
choices: That isn't gematria in any traditional sense — the system is Hebrew-letter-specific with defined methods; English ordinal numbering is a modern folk invention. And even within real gematria, a bare number-match without method, context, and tradition is the base-rate fallacy, not revelation.
They're right — the numbers don't lie.
666 is always significant.
Try Hebrew instead and it'll be meaningful.
scenarios.hint: English A=1/Z=26 'gematria' on a license plate yields 666 — is this gematria?
scenarios.why: A is correct on both counts: the method isn't traditional gematria at all, and the inference ignores base rates (with 26 letters and free word choice, 'significant' numbers are manufacturable at will). B and C surrender to the fallacy; D fixes the method but not the inference.

scenarios.title: The Golem Instructions
scenarios.situation: A popular book presents the Sefer Yetzirah as 'the golem-making manual' with step-by-step instructions. A reader tries to follow them literally.
evidence: no procedural golem instructions in any recension's plain text.
scenarios.prompt: What is the textual reality?
choices: The golem reading is commentarial tradition (medieval, notably Eleazar of Worms), not the text's plain sense — the Yetzirah itself is terse cosmogony about letters and numbers, not a how-to manual. The book collapses 800 years of commentary into the 'original,' misleading the reader about what the text is.
The instructions work if followed precisely.
The Yetzirah is entirely about golems.
Medieval commentators corrupted the pure original.
scenarios.hint: Is the Sefer Yetzirah a golem-making manual?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It distinguishes text from reception: the Yetzirah's plain sense is combinatorial cosmogony; the practical-golem reading is a later interpretive layer. Collapsing them misrepresents both. B is credulity; C inverts the text's proportions; D moralizes about a normal interpretive process.

scenarios.title: The Red String
scenarios.situation: A celebrity-endorsed organization sells red-string bracelets and 'Kabbalah classes' promising success, with no Hebrew, no textual study, and no connection to any Jewish lineage. Critics call it appropriation; defenders call it universal wisdom.
evidence: no Hebrew, no texts cited, fees for 'secret' teachings, no lineage named.
scenarios.prompt: What is the critical framework for assessing this?
choices: Ask the lineage questions: what texts, what teachers, what tradition's authority — and the transformation questions: what's kept, what's dropped, who decides? Commerce built on a tradition's name without its substance, study, or community accountability is the pattern critics identify — assess any group, including this one, by those lights.
It's all Kabbalah; gatekeeping is wrong.
Only born Jews may study Kabbalah.
Celebrities can't be spiritual.
scenarios.hint: How do you assess a commercial 'Kabbalah' organization critically but fairly?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It offers criteria rather than verdicts: lineage, textual substance, community accountability, and honest labeling of what's adapted. These assess any esoteric organization fairly — the framework doesn't prejudge, it investigates. B dissolves all distinctions; C states a false historical claim (non-Jews have studied Kabbalah for centuries, with debate); D is ad hominem.

scenarios.title: The Wellness Tree
scenarios.situation: A coaching program teaches 'the Tree of Life for executive success' — sephiroth as productivity hacks, no Hebrew, no history, no mention of any tradition. Graduates report feeling inspired.
evidence: zero Hebrew, zero texts, zero history; 'ancient secrets' marketing.
scenarios.prompt: What is the assessment?
choices: It's using the Tree's vocabulary without its substance — inspiration isn't the issue, but calling it Kabbalah/Qabalah without the textual, historical, or traditional content is mislabeling. Assess it as a coaching program (does it work?) separately from its esoteric claims (are they grounded?).
If it inspires people, the labeling doesn't matter.
All modern uses are equally valid.
Coaches shouldn't use old symbols.
scenarios.hint: A coaching program sells 'Tree of Life for executives' with no tradition — how do you assess it?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It separates two questions — pragmatic efficacy and traditional grounding — instead of letting one answer the other. Inspiration is real but doesn't establish lineage; the labeling question is about honesty, not gatekeeping. B, C dissolve the distinction; D is blanket prohibition.

domains.name: Tarot Systems
domains.description: The Fool's journey, the three great traditions, correspondences, and the craft of reading.

scenarios.title: The Tower in Every Reading
scenarios.situation: A novice reader draws the Tower and announces 'disaster is coming' in every reading where it appears — for a job interview, a vacation, a Tuesday. Querents leave frightened; the reader feels powerful.
evidence: Tower = 'disaster' in 14 consecutive readings, all contexts.
scenarios.prompt: What is the reader doing wrong?
choices: Reading the card as an isolated doom-token instead of relationally: the Tower between the Devil and the Star, in a three-card spread about a job interview, dignified by its neighbors — catastrophe is one register among several (sudden change, revelation, the lightning that illuminates). Fixed doom-meanings are the reader's power trip, not the card.
Nothing — the Tower means disaster.
They should remove the Tower from the deck.
Only read for other people, never yourself.
scenarios.hint: A reader announces doom every time the Tower appears — what is the methodological error?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The card's meaning lives in its relations — sequence position, neighboring cards, spread position, question asked. 'The Tower always means disaster' flattens a multivalent archetype into a scare device. B is the error restated; C mutilates the deck; D is irrelevant.

scenarios.title: The Court Card Confusion
scenarios.situation: A reader draws the Knight of Swords for 'how should I approach this negotiation?' and tells the querent 'a young dark-haired man will be involved.' The querent spends the meeting watching for the man instead of preparing.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong?
choices: The reader defaulted to 'court = literal person' without considering the question: for 'how should I approach,' the Knight of Swords reads as strategy — swift, direct, intellect-led action. The person-reading was possible but the question pointed to approach; the reader ignored the disambiguating context.
Nothing — court cards are always people.
The reader should have drawn another card.
Knights never mean people.
scenarios.hint: Knight of Swords for 'how should I approach this?' read as a literal man — what is the error?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Court cards' referent (person, self-facet, strategy) is resolved by the question and spread position — 'how should I approach' asks for strategy. Defaulting to literal-person regardless of question is the classic court-card error. B and D are opposite dogmatisms; C avoids the interpretive work.

scenarios.title: The Mixed Attributions
scenarios.situation: A student's notes use Thoth card names (Lust, Art), RWS numbers, and Marseille pip meanings — blended without awareness. Their readings are vivid but their study notes contradict themselves across pages.
evidence: three attribution systems blended within single spreads.
scenarios.prompt: What is the structural problem?
choices: Unconscious syncretism across three distinct systems: each deck is a coherent symbolic language, and mixing their attributions breaks each one's internal logic. The fix is sequential mastery — one deck's system completely, then comparison with the differences mapped explicitly.
They need a fourth deck.
Contradiction is the point of Tarot.
They should only read intuitively.
scenarios.hint: Notes blend Thoth names, RWS numbers, Marseille pips — what is the structural fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The decks are separate languages; code-switching mid-sentence produces the contradictions in the notes. Sequential mastery then explicit comparison preserves each system's integrity. B adds noise; C mystifies a study error; D abandons the symbolic systems that make Tarot more than inkblots.

scenarios.title: The Ancient Tarot-Kabbalah
scenarios.situation: A book claims the Tarot trumps were designed by Kabbalists in antiquity as 'a pictorial Kabbalah,' with the 22 paths as the proof. It presents the Golden Dawn table as ancient.
evidence: trumps 15th c.; path system medieval; union documented 1888-1900.
scenarios.prompt: What does the historical record show?
choices: The mapping is the Golden Dawn's late-19th-century synthesis: the trumps are 15th-century game cards, Kabbalah's path system developed independently, and their union is documented to the 1888-1900 period (Lévi's earlier work prepared it). The book backdates a modern synthesis — the table is real and useful, but not ancient.
The book is right; the scholars are biased.
Correspondences don't need history.
The Golden Dawn invented Tarot.
scenarios.hint: A book presents the GD correspondence table as ancient Kabbalistic design — what is the documented chronology?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the documented chronology: game cards (15th c.), independent Kabbalistic development, Lévi's 19th-c. preparation, the GD synthesis (1888–1900). The table's value doesn't depend on antiquity — backdating it is unnecessary and false. B dismisses evidence; C abandons the question; D overcorrects.

scenarios.title: The Weekly Dependency
scenarios.situation: A querent has been coming weekly for six months, asking the reader to decide everything — job choices, relationships, medical questions. The reader encourages it ('the cards want to guide you') and charges per session. The querent's own judgment has atrophied.
evidence: 26 weekly sessions; medical questions answered deterministically; 'the cards want to guide you'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the ethical failure?
choices: Fostering dependency for profit: the reader has replaced the querent's autonomy with a revenue stream, and is answering question types (medical especially) that are outside any reader's competence. Ethical practice builds the querent's own judgment, declines determinism on serious matters, and refers out — this is the profession's disgrace case.
Nothing — the querent chooses to come.
The reader should raise prices.
Weekly is fine; daily would be too much.
scenarios.hint: A reader has a weekly dependent asking medical questions — what are the ethical failures?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It names both failures: the dependency business model (autonomy replaced by sessions) and the competence boundary (medical/financial determinism). Consent doesn't cure exploitation when the practitioner engineers the need. B abdicates professional ethics; C and D optimize the exploitation.

scenarios.title: The Reversed Tower
scenarios.situation: The reader draws the Tower reversed in the 'outcome' position and announces 'good news — the disaster is cancelled!' The querent relaxes completely and takes no precautions about the risky situation they asked about.
evidence: question about a genuinely risky venture; outcome: Tower reversed.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this reading?
choices: Reversal-as-cancellation is the crudest reversal reading — reversed Tower more responsibly reads as the upheaval internalized, delayed, or manifesting privately; 'disaster cancelled' tells the querent what they want to hear and disarms exactly the caution the situation needs. The reader substituted reassurance for interpretation.
Nothing — reversed means the opposite.
The Tower should never be reversed.
Outcomes can't be read.
scenarios.hint: Reversed Tower in 'outcome' read as 'disaster cancelled' — what is the methodological and ethical error?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It distinguishes the responsible reversal repertoire (blocked/delayed/internalized) from the reassurance reflex, and notes the ethical dimension: the reading disarmed necessary caution. B is the error restated as method; C is dogma; D abandons the position's function.

domains.name: The Golden Dawn
domains.description: The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn: cipher manuscripts, grades, rituals, and the schism that scattered its heirs.

scenarios.title: The Sprengel Letters
scenarios.situation: A Golden Dawn lineage group advertises 'direct charter descent from Fraulein Sprengel's German order' as proof of legitimacy. A prospective member asks whether this claim is historically solid.
evidence: Sprengel letters exist in copies; no German order verified; forgery alleged but unproven.
scenarios.prompt: What is the accurate answer?
choices: The Sprengel correspondence is disputed and the German order was never independently verified — Crowley alleged forgery, and no German temple materialized. The claim is tradition, not documented history; a group's legitimacy rests on its teaching and practice, not on an unverifiable 1888 charter story.
The charter is proven; the skeptics are biased.
It doesn't matter at all.
Only German orders are legitimate.
scenarios.hint: A group claims Sprengel-charter legitimacy — is the claim historically solid?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It states the evidential situation plainly (disputed letters, unverified order) without taking the forgery allegation as proven either, and redirects legitimacy to what can be evaluated — teaching quality and practice. B asserts what isn't established; C abandons the historical question; D invents a criterion.

scenarios.title: The Instant Adept
scenarios.situation: An online order offers 'Adeptus Minor initiation' for $499, no prior grades, no examination, immediate delivery. Their site displays the full grade table.
evidence: 'immediate Adeptus Minor, no prerequisites, $499, certificate included'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the critical assessment?
choices: The grades are curriculum markers for examined, sequential work — selling the title without the curriculum inverts the system's logic. The grade table on the site describes what the buyer isn't getting. Evaluate esoteric groups by what advancement actually requires, not what titles they display.
It's a bargain; traditional orders are gatekeeping.
Grades don't matter anyway.
Only the price is wrong.
scenarios.hint: Adeptus Minor for $499, no curriculum — what does the system's own logic say?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It applies the system's own logic: grades mark completed examined work, so selling the marker without the work is incoherent by the tradition's standards. The assessment criterion (what does advancement require?) generalizes to any group. B mistakes commerce for access; C dismisses the structure; D haggling misses the point.

scenarios.title: The Oath Question
scenarios.situation: A student discovers Regardie published the Order's secret papers and asks: 'Was he wrong to break his oath? And am I wrong to study the published material?'
evidence: Regardie's 1937-40 publication vs. initiates' objections; system survived via the breach.
scenarios.prompt: What is the thoughtful response?
choices: Both questions deserve the tension, not a slogan: the publication broke real trust and real oaths — and it preserved a system that would otherwise have fragmented into rumor. Studying published material is legitimate (it's published), but the student should understand what the secrecy was for (transmission integrity, graded readiness) and what its loss cost. Hold both truths.
Oaths are meaningless; read everything.
He was a traitor; burn the books.
Secrets should never be published.
scenarios.hint: Was Regardie wrong to publish — and is studying the material wrong?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It refuses both the libertarian shrug and the traditionalist condemnation, instead articulating what was actually at stake on each side — trust versus preservation, graded transmission versus public access. The student is given a framework for judgment, not a verdict to parrot. B, C, D are all slogans.

scenarios.title: The Daily Pentagrams
scenarios.situation: A practitioner has performed the LBRP daily for a year 'because you're supposed to' but can't say what any element means — the god-names are sounds, the quarters are directions. They report no effects and growing boredom.
evidence: 'I do the pentagrams every morning'; cannot name the god-names' attributions.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis?
choices: Practice without the correspondence system: the ritual is the Lectures made physical — the god-names invoke specific sephirothic forces, the quarters carry elemental attributions. Performed as empty routine it's calisthenics; studied as applied Kabbalah it's the tradition's laboratory. The fix is study, not more repetitions.
They need to do it twice daily.
The ritual doesn't work.
Boredom means it's working.
scenarios.hint: A year of daily LBRP with no understanding and no effects — what is the diagnosis?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The LBRP's efficacy in the tradition's own terms depends on the practitioner's informed engagement with what each element invokes — the system is designed as theory-practice unity. B prescribes more of the failing approach; C judges without the required preparation; D mystifies the problem.

scenarios.title: Whose Golden Dawn?
scenarios.situation: Three contemporary groups each claim to be 'the' Golden Dawn: one with initiatory lineage through the Stella Matutina, one reconstructed purely from Regardie's books, one founded last year with new channeled material added. A seeker asks which is authentic.
evidence: lineage vs reconstruction vs innovation; all use the name.
scenarios.prompt: What framework answers this?
choices: Lineage is one input, not the verdict: ask what each transmits (which papers? which practices? examined how?), how authority works (checked or absolute?), and whether additions are labeled as additions. 'Authentic' dissolves into specific, answerable questions — the seeker can then choose by their own criteria instead of outsourcing judgment to a trademark.
The oldest lineage wins automatically.
The book-reconstructed one is inauthentic.
New channeled material is always illegitimate.
scenarios.hint: Three groups claim the Golden Dawn name — how does a seeker evaluate them?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It replaces the unanswerable 'which is THE Golden Dawn' with investigable questions about transmission, practice, and governance — the same criteria historians use. The seeker gets tools, not a ruling. B, C, D each assert a single criterion as decisive, which is precisely the kind of authority-claim the schism should make one suspicious of.

scenarios.title: The Unquestionable Contact
scenarios.situation: A contemporary teacher claims guidance from a discarnate master who 'confirms' the teacher's decisions — including financial ones affecting students. Questioning students are told their doubt proves they're 'not ready.'
evidence: 'the Master confirms'; doubters labeled unready; fees involved.
scenarios.prompt: What is the structural analysis?
choices: Unverifiable authority deployed as a dispute-closer with a built-in defense against questioning (doubt = unreadiness) — the Mathers pattern exactly. The financial dimension raises the stakes: assess by the portable questions — what independently verifies the claims, who can question, what happens when they do — and note that 'doubt proves unreadiness' is a thought-terminating cliché, not an answer.
Disprove the master's existence.
The students should just trust.
All spiritual teachers are frauds.
scenarios.hint: A teacher's discarnate master 'confirms' financial decisions; doubters are 'not ready' — what is the analysis?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It applies the organizational analysis without needing to settle metaphysics, identifies the thought-terminating defense mechanism, and flags the financial stakes. B demands proof of a negative; C surrenders judgment; D overgeneralizes from the pattern.

domains.name: Chaos Magic
domains.description: Belief as a tool, sigils, gnosis, and servitors — the postmodern magic of Austin Osman Spare's heirs.

scenarios.title: The Dabbler's Grimoire
scenarios.situation: A practitioner collects initiations, paradigms, and systems — a weekend workshop here, a PDF grimoire there — but has never sustained any practice longer than a month. They cite 'paradigm shifting' as their method.
evidence: 12 systems sampled; longest sustained practice: 3 weeks; no journal.
scenarios.prompt: What is the critique from within chaos magic itself?
choices: They're paradigm-touring, not paradigm-shifting: the method requires inhabiting each paradigm deeply enough to believe it fully and produce results — Carroll's own writing insists on this. Collecting systems without sustained practice is the exact failure mode the tradition warns against; 'nothing is true' was never permission for 'nothing is learned deeply.'
They need more paradigms.
Chaos magic has no standards, so it's fine.
They should pick one religion permanently.
scenarios.hint: A 'chaos magician' collects systems but practices none deeply — what does the tradition itself say?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It applies the tradition's internal standard: paradigm shifting is a discipline of deep temporary belief, and the dabbler fails that standard by the tradition's own criteria. B prescribes more of the disease; C mistakes anti-authoritarianism for anti-standards; D inverts the method entirely.

scenarios.title: The Unforgotten Sigil
scenarios.situation: A practitioner creates sigils daily, photographs them, posts them, and checks hourly for results. Nothing manifests. They conclude sigil magic doesn't work.
evidence: no gnosis, no banishing, hourly outcome-checking, sigils shared publicly.
scenarios.prompt: What does the method say went wrong?
choices: They violated the structural requirements: charging without gnosis (no altered state, just wishing), and the forgetting/banishing step inverted — hourly result-checking is maximal lust of result, which the theory identifies as the interference mechanism. The method wasn't tested; its preconditions were ignored.
The intents were wrong.
Sigils need better art.
They need more sigils per day.
scenarios.hint: Daily sigils, posted and result-checked hourly, 'don't work' — what does the method diagnose?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It distinguishes testing the method from violating its stated preconditions — gnosis-charging and forgetting aren't optional flourishes, they're the theory's load-bearing elements. Judging the method by this practice is like judging a recipe never followed. B, C, D all miss the structural point.

scenarios.title: The Shortcut Seeker
scenarios.situation: A newcomer asks for 'the fastest gnosis method' and is pointed by a forum to breath-restriction techniques from the literature's fringes. They ask you whether to try it.
evidence: recommending asphyxia-adjacent techniques to a beginner.
scenarios.prompt: What is the responsible answer?
choices: No — the dangerous fringes are not the curriculum: inhibitory meditation and ordinary excitatory methods (breathwork, movement) reach the functional state safely, and the tradition's responsible voices are explicit that injury-risking methods are bad tools. 'Fastest' is the wrong optimization; safe and repeatable is.
Try it once; you'll be fine.
Faster is better in magic.
Only with a partner.
scenarios.hint: A newcomer asks about breath-restriction gnosis from the fringes — what is the responsible answer?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It refuses the premise ('fastest') and redirects to the safe core, citing the tradition's own responsible voices — this isn't external moralizing but internal standard-keeping. B, C gamble with safety; D mitigates without addressing the core issue.

scenarios.title: The Servitor That Wouldn't Die
scenarios.situation: A practitioner launched a servitor for 'confidence in meetings' two years ago with no lifespan and no decommissioning plan. They now report intrusive 'presence' experiences and can't seem to stop it. They're frightened.
evidence: 2-year-old servitor, no decommissioning plan, intrusive experiences.
scenarios.prompt: What does the tradition prescribe?
choices: The decommissioning that should have been planned: a formal dissolution rite — thanking, reabsorbing, or banishing the form, in gnosis, with clear intent — plus the psychological work (the 'presence' may be an autonomous complex needing integration, not just banishing). And the general lesson: lifecycle management is part of the method, not an afterthought.
It's permanent; live with it.
Stronger banishing, repeatedly, forever.
It was never real; ignore it.
scenarios.hint: A servitor launched without lifespan or kill switch now feels autonomous — what is the prescription?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives both the traditional remedy (formal dissolution, which should have been pre-planned) and the psychological dimension (autonomous complexes need integration), treating the practitioner's experience seriously while providing method. B surrenders; C escalates without resolving; D gaslights the experiencer.

scenarios.title: The Quantum Claim

lessons.title: The Seven Principles as a System of Interpretation
concepts: The seven principles come to us from The Kybalion (1908), published under the byline 'Three Initiates' and commonly attributed by scholars to William Walker Atkinson. They belong to the early-20th-century occult revival, not to the ancient Corpus Hermeticum. This is not a demotion: it simply tells us what kind of source we are reading — modern interpretive tradition — so we can study it honestly.

Mentalism ('THE ALL is MIND; The Universe is Mental') is presented as the master key: the claim that reality is fundamentally mental, and that disciplined mind is therefore the first instrument of the student. Every other principle is read through this root.

Correspondence ('As above, so below') is a method of analogical reading: patterns on one plane illuminate patterns on another. Vibration ('Nothing rests; everything moves') universalizes motion; Polarity ('opposites are identical in nature, but different in degree') structures it as a scale; Rhythm ('everything flows, out and in') describes its swing; Cause and Effect ('chance is but a name for law not recognized') denies causeless events; Gender describes generation through the union of projective and receptive principles on all planes.

The tradition insists the principles interlock: Correspondence without Mentalism is fortune-telling by analogy; Polarity without Rhythm is a static scale; Causation without Correspondence cannot read the chain across planes. Study them as one instrument with seven registers, not seven separate tools.

A standing caution: the 1908 text predates the mature quantum theory it is sometimes said to anticipate, and modern commentary that merges the principles with physics is a 20th–21st-century phenomenon worth studying as commentary — not as evidence of what the text itself establishes.

The practical posture of the Kybalion tradition is contemplative rather than manipulative: observe the principle in experience, trace its operation, and work with its law rather than against it. The exercises in this path follow that posture — journaling, symbolic reading, and slow analysis rather than any claim of supernatural technique.

example.code: "Like and unlike are the same; opposites are identical in nature, but different in degree; extremes meet; all truths are but half-truths; all paradoxes may be reconciled." — The Kybalion (1908), the axiom of Polarity
example.walkthrough: Work the axiom clause by clause. 'Opposites are identical in nature, but different in degree' is the core: fear and courage are not two substances but one scale. 'Extremes meet' follows: push far enough along the scale and you arrive at the far pole — the tradition's basis for transmutation of mental states. 'All truths are but half-truths' is the epistemic humility the principle demands: any one pole is only half the scale. A correct contemplative use: locate your current state on the scale (say, at 'fear'), acknowledge it as a degree rather than a destiny, and practice moving the degree — the tradition's 'sliding' along the pole — rather than declaring war on an enemy.

pitfalls: Treating the principles as ancient: they are 1908 interpretive tradition; attributing them to Hermes Trismegistus himself is historically false.
Literalizing Correspondence into mechanical determinism ('the stars control my liver') — the tradition means analogical likeness, not physical causation.
Merging Vibration with modern physics and calling it 'confirmed' — analogy is not confirmation, and the chronology runs the wrong way.
Reading Gender as biological essentialism — the text's own framing distinguishes the metaphysical principles of generation from physical sex.
Using Polarity as positive thinking: the principle is about the structure of opposites, not about denying the low end of the scale.

lessons.title: From Alexandria to the Renaissance: A History of the Hermetic Texts
concepts: Hermes Trismegistus is a syncretic figure — the Hellenistic fusion of the Greek Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth, gods of writing, wisdom, and mediation — not a single documented historical author. The Hermetica are a composite literature of the Greco-Egyptian world, attributed to his authority.

The Corpus Hermeticum is a collection of seventeen Greek treatises (plus the Latin Asclepius, a dialogue surviving in Latin, and fragments preserved by Stobaeus). Its most famous treatise, the Poimandres (CH I), presents a vision received by Hermes from the divine Mind — a cosmogony in the service of gnosis, the direct knowing by which the soul ascends.

Isaac Casaubon's 1614 demonstration remains the hinge of Hermetic scholarship: the Corpus belongs to the 1st–3rd centuries CE, not to a Mosaic antiquity. The redating moved the texts from legend into history — the real world of Roman Egypt, where Greek philosophy met Egyptian religion — and made them seriously studiable.

The Emerald Tablet's documentary trail begins not in an Egyptian tomb but in Arabic sources (the Kitāb Sirr al-Khalīqa, c. 8th–9th century) and medieval Latin translations. Its thirteen lines gave alchemy its most quoted maxim and closed with the 'threefold wisdom' — read in tradition as alchemy, astrology, and theurgy.

The Renaissance recovery ran through Florence: Cosimo de' Medici's 1460 manuscript and Marsilio Ficino's Latin translation (printed 1471) made Hermes a household name in learned Europe, feeding Renaissance Platonism, the prisca theologia framework, and early modern natural philosophy — Paracelsus in medicine, John Dee in mathematics and angel magic, the Rosicrucian manifestos from 1614.

The modern line runs through the 19th-century occult revival — Eliphas Lévi, the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn (1888), New Thought — and culminates for our purposes in The Kybalion (1908). The responsible student keeps the layers distinct: late-antique primary texts, medieval alchemical classics, Renaissance reception, and modern interpretation are different strata of one tradition.

example.code: "That which is below is like that which is above, and that which is above is like that which is below, to accomplish the miracles of the one thing." — the Emerald Tablet, in Isaac Newton's English rendering of the Latin
example.walkthrough: Read the sentence as the tradition reads it: a claim of likeness ('like'), not identity or causation. The 'miracles of the one thing' names the tablet's alchemy: the one matter worked through its correspondences. Historically, place the line correctly: you are reading a medieval Latin text translated from Arabic sources (8th–9th century), rendered into early modern English by Newton — four layers of transmission. Contemplatively, the line is the root of the Correspondence principle: the invitation to read the lower by the higher. Keep all three readings — textual, historical, contemplative — in play at once; the tradition's best readers always did.

pitfalls: Calling the Corpus Hermeticum a work of Moses' contemporary: Renaissance readers believed this; Casaubon (1614) and modern scholarship place the treatises in the 1st–3rd centuries CE.
Presenting the Emerald Tablet as an ancient Egyptian artifact: the documentary record begins with Arabic and medieval Latin transmission; the tomb-discovery story is legend.
Treating The Kybalion (1908) as an ancient primary source: it is a modern interpretive work of the occult revival.
Reading John Dee's angel magic as disproving his mathematics (or vice versa): before the modern science/esotericism divide, Hermeticism was a live idiom of natural philosophy.
Assuming 'as above, so below' is the tablet's exact wording: it is a summary of the opening maxim; the transmitted texts say 'like that which is above.'

lessons.title: Zosimos of Panopolis: The Alexandrian Roots
concepts: Zosimos of Panopolis (c. 300 CE) is the earliest alchemical author whose works survive in substantial form — writing in Greek in Roman Egypt, at the intersection of Egyptian temple craft, Greek philosophy, and early metallurgy. His writings describe real laboratory apparatus (the kerotakis, the tribikos still) alongside visionary dream-sequences, establishing the pattern that defines alchemy: material practice fused with spiritual interpretation.

The Alexandrian context matters: the Museum and Library made Alexandria the ancient world's research hub, and its workshops produced genuine chemical knowledge — distillation, sublimation, alloying, dyeing. Alchemy grew from craft practitioners theorizing about their materials, not from philosophers speculating abstractly. The 'sacred art' (cheimeia) was workshop knowledge first.

Zosimos's famous vision of the 'priest of the inner sanctuaries' being boiled alive in a cauldron — interpreted as the metals suffering transformation — shows the symbolic reading layered over physical process. This double vision (the metal and the soul transformed together) is the core alchemical move: outer work mirrors inner work, and the laboratory becomes a theater of spiritual change.

What survives and how: Zosimos reaches us through Byzantine manuscript compilations (notably the Marcianus Graecus 299), copied and recopied for a millennium. The transmission history itself is a lesson in critical reading — later copyists added, rearranged, and attributed, so 'Zosimos says' always requires asking which manuscript, which recension, which century's hand.

example.code:
Alexandrian alchemy (c. 100-400 CE) -- key figures & texts
  Pseudo-Democritus ..... recipe collections (metallurgy, dyeing)
  Maria the Jewess ...... kerotakis, tribikos, 'bain-marie' namesake
  Zosimos of Panopolis . earliest substantial author; visions + apparatus
  Synesius .............. commentary bridging craft and philosophy
Transmission: Greek originals -> Byzantine compilations (10th c. mss)
              -> Arabic translations (8th-9th c.) -> Latin West (12th c.)
example.walkthrough: The timeline places Zosimos in a living tradition — recipe-writers before him, commentators after — and traces the thousand-year transmission chain that carries Alexandrian alchemy to the Latin West. Each arrow is a translation event where material was preserved, transformed, or misattributed, which is why the critical-reading domain's tools apply directly to alchemical texts.

pitfalls: Treating alchemy as 'failed chemistry': it was a different project — material-spiritual transformation — and judging it by modern chemistry's goals misses what it actually did and knew.
Reading visions literally or dismissing them: Zosimos's boiling-priest is neither a lab report nor nonsense — it's symbolic exegesis of process; both literalist readings fail.
Ignoring the transmission chain: quoting 'Zosimos' from a 16th-century Latin compilation as if it were his 3rd-century Greek words — always ask which manuscript.
lessons.try_it: Read a summary of Zosimos's visions (available in public-domain translations). Write one paragraph on what the boiling-priest vision says about process, and one on what it says about the alchemist.

lessons.title: Jabir ibn Hayyan & Islamic Alchemy
concepts: The Arabic alchemical corpus attributed to Jabir ibn Hayyan (Geber, 8th century) is among the largest bodies of alchemical writing ever produced — hundreds of treatises covering laboratory technique, cosmology, numerology, and the famous sulfur-mercury theory of metals. Modern scholarship debates whether one man wrote them (the 'Jabir problem' parallels the Homeric question), but the corpus's influence is undoubted.

The sulfur-mercury theory: all metals are composed of sulfur and mercury in varying purities and proportions — gold is the perfect balance, base metals the imbalanced. Transmutation becomes a medical model: purify the 'sick' metal as a physician purifies the body. This theory dominated Western alchemy for 700 years after its 12th-century Latin translation.

The Islamic alchemists' laboratory legacy is concrete: Jabirian texts describe distillation apparatus, crystallization, calcination, and sublimation with unprecedented precision — and Arabic alchemy gives chemistry its vocabulary (alembic, alcohol, alkali, elixir all pass through Arabic). The experimental emphasis — 'the first essential is that you should perform practical work' — is the corpus's methodological gift.

The Jabir problem as critical-reading exercise: texts attributed to one 8th-century figure show multiple authorial voices, anachronistic references, and centuries of accretion. Dating by internal evidence (terminology, cited authorities, doctrinal development) versus traditional attribution is exactly the pseudepigrapha analysis the critical-reading domain teaches.

example.code:
Jabirian sulfur-mercury theory (simplified)
  sulfur (hot, dry, active) + mercury (cold, moist, passive)
     | varying purity & proportion |
     v                             v
  GOLD (perfect balance)    LEAD (gross imbalance)
Transmutation = purification: remove the 'sickness' (impurity),
restore balance -- a medical model applied to metals.
Arabic gifts to chemistry's vocabulary:
  alembic, alcohol, alkali, elixir, realgar, tutty
example.walkthrough: The diagram reduces the sulfur-mercury theory to its logic: metals as compounds of two principles, transmutation as purification — the medical model that made alchemy intellectually respectable for centuries. The vocabulary list shows the concrete linguistic legacy: modern chemistry still speaks Arabic in its glassware and reagents.

pitfalls: The 'Jabir problem' as trivia: it's a method lesson — attributed authorship vs internal evidence is the core critical-reading skill, applicable to every esoteric corpus.
Reading sulfur-mercury as bad chemistry: it was a coherent theoretical framework that organized 700 years of practice — judge theories by their fruitfulness, not just their truth.
Ignoring the laboratory content: the corpus's lasting contribution is experimental method and apparatus, not just theory.
lessons.try_it: Take one Jabirian laboratory description (distillation). Rewrite it as a modern lab procedure — then note what the original's cosmological framing adds that the modern version loses.

lessons.title: Paracelsus: Spagyrics & Iatrochemistry
concepts: Paracelsus (Philippus von Hohenheim, 1493–1541) — the bombastic Swiss physician who burned the medical textbooks in public — redirected alchemy from metals to medicine: iatrochemistry, chemistry in the service of healing. Disease, he argued, was chemical imbalance treatable by chemically prepared remedies; the physician must be an alchemist.

Spagyrics (from Greek spao, 'to separate,' and ageiro, 'to combine') is his method: separate a plant into its components (through distillation, extraction, calcination), purify each, then recombine them into a medicine 'exalted' beyond the crude herb. The tria prima — sulfur, mercury, salt as the three principles of all bodies — gave the separation its theoretical targets.

The legacy is double-edged: Paracelsus founded pharmaceutical chemistry (dose makes the poison — 'sola dosis facit venenum' — is his), yet his cosmology of signatures, arcana, and astral influences reads as occult. Both are genuinely his; the critical reader holds both without forcing a choice between 'scientist' and 'mystic.'

The spagyric revival (19th–20th century, and today's herbalist movement) shows the tradition's persistence — and the critical question it raises: which claims are testable pharmacology and which are cosmological framing? The respectful reader distinguishes the registers without dismissing either.

example.code:
Spagyric method (Paracelsian)
  1. SEPARATE (spao) .... distill / extract / calcinate the plant
                            -> tria prima: sulfur (oil/soul),
                               mercury (spirit), salt (body)
  2. PURIFY .............. cleanse each principle of 'impurity'
  3. COHOBATE (ageiro) ... recombine the purified principles
                            -> the 'exalted' medicine
  Paracelsian maxim: 'sola dosis facit venenum'
  (only the dose makes the poison -- foundation of toxicology)
example.walkthrough: The spagyric sequence shows the method behind the mystique: separation, purification, recombination — each step a real laboratory operation mapped onto the tria prima theory. The dose maxim at the bottom is the bridge to modernity: the same man who read astral signatures founded toxicology's central principle.

pitfalls: Forcing Paracelsus into 'scientist' or 'mystic': he was both, inextricably — the critical reader holds the tension rather than resolving it by amputation.
Dismissing spagyrics as pre-scientific: the method (separate, purify, recombine) is genuine pharmaceutical technique; the cosmology is the interpretive frame.
Uncritical revivalism: modern spagyric claims need the same evidence standards as any pharmacology — tradition is not data.
lessons.try_it: Research one Paracelsian remedy with modern pharmacology in mind: what was the active principle (if any), and what did the cosmology add or obscure?

lessons.title: Newton the Alchemist: The Hidden Manuscripts
concepts: Isaac Newton wrote more about alchemy and theology than about physics — over a million words of alchemical manuscripts, hidden during his life and barely studied until the 20th century. The author of the Principia spent decades in the laboratory trying to understand the vegetative growth of metals, copying alchemical treatises by hand, and developing his own symbolic vocabulary.

The manuscripts show a systematic researcher: Newton's alchemical notebooks (now largely digitized, as the Newton Project) contain careful experimental records, cross-referenced reading notes, and chronological study plans. He approached alchemy with the same methodical intensity as optics — the 'rationalist magus' was one person, not two.

The historiographic lesson: the Newton of the textbooks (pure rationalist) versus the Newton of the manuscripts (alchemist-theologian) — the first is a 19th-century invention, the second is the archive. The 'two Newtons' problem teaches that historical figures are pruned to fit narratives, and the pruning always serves somebody's story about what counts as legitimate knowledge.

What Newton sought in alchemy: not gold, but the active principles behind nature's operations — the same quest that produced gravity. His alchemy and his physics ask one question: what are the hidden forces by which matter transforms? Reading them together (as scholars like Betty Jo Teeter Dobbs did) gives the complete Newton.

example.code:
Newton's unpublished corpus (order of magnitude)
  physics & mathematics ......... ~1M words published
  alchemy ....................... ~1M words (manuscript, hidden)
  theology & prophecy ........... ~1M+ words (manuscript, hidden)
  optics ........................ substantial, published late
The 'Newton' of textbooks = the published third.
The Newton Project (newtonproject.org) has digitized the manuscripts;
the hidden two-thirds are now readable -- and change the story.
example.walkthrough: The word counts make the point quantitatively: the published physicist is roughly a third of the writer. The Newton Project's digitization is the critical event — the hidden manuscripts moved from rumor to readable archive, letting anyone verify the claims. The lesson generalizes: check what the archive actually contains before accepting the textbook portrait.

pitfalls: The 'embarrassment' reading: treating Newton's alchemy as a shameful hobby — it was central to his inquiry into nature's active principles, pursued with full methodical rigor.
Using Newton to legitimize anything: 'Newton did alchemy, therefore alchemy is true' — the manuscripts prove he did it, not that it worked.
Ignoring the archive: opining about Newton's beliefs without reading the digitized manuscripts — the Newton Project made the primary sources public; use them.
lessons.try_it: Browse the Newton Project's alchemical manuscripts. Pick one notebook page: transcribe what he's doing (experiment? copying? theorizing?) and note the methodical features.

lessons.title: The Misattributed Manuscript
concepts: The alchemical corpus is a thicket of pseudepigrapha — texts attributed to Hermes, Democritus, Plato, Aristotle, and later to Jabir, Aquinas, and Llull, most written centuries after their supposed authors. Attribution was a claim to authority, not a record of authorship: 'Hermes says' meant 'this is ancient wisdom,' and the name did argumentative work the content couldn't do alone.

Dating tools: terminology (when did this technical term enter use?), cited authorities (you can't cite someone born after you), doctrinal development (theories evolve — sulfur-mercury has a history), manuscript witnesses (oldest surviving copy sets the latest possible date), and material evidence (paper, ink, binding for physical manuscripts). Each gives a constraint; together they triangulate.

The respectful stance: pseudepigrapha aren't frauds in the modern sense — the authors participated in a tradition where speaking as Hermes was a way of speaking with the tradition's voice. Condemning them as forgeries imports a modern authorship concept; the critical reader notes the attribution practice without either credulity or moralism.

Case method: take any famous attribution (the Emerald Tablet's 'Hermes Trismegistus,' the Aquinas alchemical treatises) and run the dating tools. The exercise teaches the general skill — and the general humility: most of what we 'know' about ancient authorship is tradition, not evidence.

example.code:
Dating toolkit (apply in order)
  1. terminology .... first-use dates of technical terms
  2. citations ...... latest cited author = earliest possible date
  3. doctrine ....... where in the theory's development does it sit?
  4. manuscripts .... oldest witness = latest possible composition date
  5. material ....... paper/ink/binding (physical mss only)
Example: a 'Hermetic' text citing Jabir (8th c.) cannot predate the 8th c.
         -- whatever 'Hermes' says on the title page.
example.walkthrough: The toolkit is ordered by ease and power: terminology and citations are desk work, doctrine requires subject knowledge, manuscripts require archive access, material analysis requires a lab. The example shows the logic at its simplest — a single anachronistic citation collapses a grandiose attribution, no matter what the title page claims.

pitfalls: Credulity toward title pages: the attribution is the claim under investigation, not evidence for itself — never date by the ascription.
Moralizing about pseudepigrapha: 'forgery!' imports modern authorship norms — understand the attribution practice before judging it.
Single-tool dating: one anachronism is suggestive, triangulation is conclusive — run the full toolkit.
lessons.try_it: Pick a famous esoteric attribution (Emerald Tablet, a 'Platonic' dialogue, a grimoire). Run the terminology + citation checks and write up the dating argument in 300 words.

lessons.title: The Tree of Life: Ten Sephiroth
concepts: The Tree of Life (Etz Chaim) is Kabbalah's master diagram: ten sephiroth (emanations) arranged in three columns, mapping how the infinite (Ein Sof) articulates itself into the structured world — and, by correspondence, how consciousness is structured. It is simultaneously cosmology, psychology, and a filing system for all correspondences.

The ten, top to bottom: Kether (Crown — pure being), Chokmah (Wisdom — the initial flash), Binah (Understanding — form given to the flash), Chesed (Mercy — expansion), Geburah (Severity — contraction), Tiphareth (Beauty — the balanced center), Netzach (Victory — endurance), Hod (Glory — intellect/form), Yesod (Foundation — the interface), Malkuth (Kingdom — the material world). Each is a lens; the Tree is the instrument.

The three columns: the right Pillar of Mercy (Chokmah, Chesed, Netzach — expansive force), the left Pillar of Severity (Binah, Geburah, Hod — restrictive force), the middle Pillar of Mildness (Kether, Tiphareth, Yesod, Malkuth — balance). Imbalance in either direction is pathology — too much mercy dissolves boundaries, too much severity crushes life. The middle pillar is the path of integration.

The four worlds overlay the Tree: Atziluth (emanation), Briah (creation), Yetzirah (formation), Assiah (action) — the same ten sephiroth operating at four levels of density. This fractal structure (each sephirah contains a whole Tree) is why Kabbalists speak of 'the Tree in the Tree' — the diagram scales from cosmos to psyche to a single decision.

example.code:
The Tree of Life (simplified)
              Kether (1)
        Chokmah (2) | Binah (3)
   Chesed (4)  Tiphareth (6)  Geburah (5)
        Netzach (7) | Hod (8)
              Yesod (9)
             Malkuth (10)
Right pillar: Mercy (2-4-7) | Left pillar: Severity (3-5-8)
Middle pillar: Mildness (1-6-9-10) -- the path of balance.
Four worlds: Atziluth > Briah > Yetzirah > Assiah (emanation to action).
example.walkthrough: The diagram lays out the ten sephiroth in their three pillars, with the middle pillar highlighted as the balancing path. The four worlds beneath show the Tree's fractal nature — the same structure from cosmic emanation down to material action. Students should memorize the positions first; the meanings deepen with use, which is why the Tree functions as a lifelong filing system.

pitfalls: Memorizing names without positions: the Tree's power is structural — the relationships (pillars, paths) carry the meaning, not the vocabulary list.
Literalizing the diagram: the sephiroth are lenses/emanations, not places or gods — reifying them into a pantheon is the classic beginner error.
Ignoring the pillars: reading sephiroth in isolation misses the Tree's core teaching — balance between the forces, via the middle.
lessons.try_it: Draw the Tree of Life from memory: ten circles, three pillars, numbered. Check against the diagram; repeat until the structure is automatic.

lessons.title: The 22 Paths & the Hebrew Letters
concepts: The 22 paths connect the ten sephiroth, and each path corresponds to a letter of the Hebrew alphabet — making the Tree a linguistic machine: the letters are the channels through which the sephirothic forces flow. The Sefer Yetzirah's letter-cosmology (letters as the building blocks of reality) is the theoretical foundation.

The letters divide into three mothers (Aleph, Mem, Shin — air, water, fire; the elements), seven doubles (planets — each with two pronunciations, hard/soft, hence 'double'), and twelve simples (zodiac signs). This 3-7-12 structure organizes the entire correspondence system: every path carries its letter's elemental, planetary, or zodiacal attribution.

Pathworking as a method: the paths are also meditative routes — the practitioner 'travels' from sephirah to sephirah along a path, encountering its letter, its Tarot trump (in the Hermetic attribution), and its symbolism. Whether read as psychology or metaphysics, it's a structured imagination exercise with a fixed symbolic vocabulary.

The critical note: the letter-path correspondences stabilized over centuries and differ between schools (the Hermetic/Qabalistic attributions of the Golden Dawn differ from earlier arrangements in places). 'The' correspondence table is always some school's table — know whose you're using.

example.code:
The 22 letters on the Tree (3-7-12 division)
  3 MOTHERS:  Aleph (air) -- Mem (water) -- Shin (fire)
  7 DOUBLES:  Beth, Gimel, Daleth, Kaph, Pe, Resh, Tav (planets)
  12 SIMPLES: He, Vav, Zayin, Cheth, Teth, Yod, Lamed, Nun,
               Samekh, Ayin, Tzaddi, Qoph (zodiac)
  3 + 7 + 12 = 22 paths. Each path = a letter = a channel
  between two sephiroth, carrying elemental/planetary/zodiacal force.
example.walkthrough: The 3-7-12 division shows the alphabet's internal cosmology: mothers for elements, doubles for planets, simples for zodiac — the same structure that organizes the paths. The equation at the bottom (3+7+12=22) is the mnemonic; the channel concept (letters as conduits between sephiroth) is the functional understanding that makes pathworking coherent.

pitfalls: Treating correspondences as universal: the Golden Dawn's letter-path-Tarot table is one school's synthesis — earlier and later arrangements differ; cite your source.
Letters as decoration: the paths' letters are functional (channels of specific forces), not labels — the 3-7-12 structure is the content.
Skipping the Hebrew: the system is built on the alphabet's shapes, sounds, and numbers — transliteration-only study misses the material.
lessons.try_it: Memorize the 3 mothers and 7 doubles with their attributions. Then trace three paths on your Tree diagram, naming each path's letter and what it connects.

lessons.title: Gematria: Number as Language
concepts: Gematria is the alphanumeric code at Kabbalah's heart: each Hebrew letter has a numerical value (Aleph=1, Beth=2 ... Yod=10, Kaph=20 ... Qoph=100, etc.), so every word is also a number, and words sharing a number share — the tradition claims — a hidden resonance. It's exegesis by arithmetic: the text's numbers are a second text.

The methods: standard (mispar hechrechi — the face values), ordinal (mispar siduri — Aleph=1 through Tav=22), reduced (mispar katan — digital roots, mod 9), and the letter-name expansions (milui — spelling out each letter's name and summing those). Different methods, different resonances — and the choice of method is itself interpretive.

The famous examples: the serpent (nachash, 358) and the messiah (mashiach, 358) share a number — a resonance the tradition reads deeply. Whether one finds this profound or coincidental is the critical question gematria always poses: with enough methods and a large lexicon, collisions are statistically inevitable — which ones mean something?

The disciplined approach: gematria as a meditative/exegetical tool within a tradition that constrains it (specific methods, textual context, doctrinal coherence) versus gematria as free association. The first is a discipline; the second is numerology-flavored pareidolia. The student learns the methods rigorously — and the skepticism rigorously too.

example.code:
Hebrew letter values (standard mispar hechrechi, abbreviated)
  Aleph=1 Beth=2 Gimel=3 Daleth=4 He=5 Vav=6 Zayin=7 Cheth=8 Teth=9
  Yod=10 Kaph=20 Lamed=30 Mem=40 Nun=50 Samekh=60 Ayin=70 Pe=80
  Tzaddi=90 Qoph=100 Resh=200 Shin=300 Tav=400
  Example: nachash (serpent) = 50+8+300 = 358
           mashiach (messiah) = 40+300+10+8 = 358
example.walkthrough: The value table is the working tool — every gematria calculation starts here. The worked example (serpent = messiah = 358) shows both the method (letter-by-letter summation) and the interpretive payoff the tradition claims. The walkthrough's closing point is the critical balance: learn the arithmetic cold, and hold the statistical skepticism equally cold.

pitfalls: Method-shopping: trying all four methods until one gives a 'meaningful' number — that's data dredging; declare the method before calculating.
Ignoring base rates: with thousands of words and four methods, collisions are guaranteed — significance needs more than a shared number.
Gematria without Hebrew: English 'gematria' (A=1, B=2...) is a modern invention with no traditional standing — the system is Hebrew-specific.
lessons.try_it: Calculate the standard gematria of three Hebrew words you choose. Then apply the base-rate test: how many other common words share one of those values? Write up what, if anything, the collision means.

lessons.title: Sefer Yetzirah: The Book of Formation
concepts: The Sefer Yetzirah (Book of Formation/Creation), likely composed between the 3rd and 6th centuries CE, is the oldest extant Kabbalistic text — and one of the strangest: a terse, almost mathematical cosmogony in which God creates the world with 32 paths of wisdom (the ten sephiroth plus the 22 letters) through combination, permutation, and 'engraving.'

Its core doctrine: the ten sephiroth beli mah ('without anything' — abstract, without substance) and the 22 letters as the building blocks — 'He engraved them, He hewed them, He combined them, He weighed them, He interchanged them.' Creation is linguistic-combinatorial: reality is spelled, and the letters' permutations generate the world's diversity.

The golem tradition grows from its margins: the commentarial tradition (notably Eleazar of Worms) reads the letter-combinations as practical instructions — form the combinations, and form follows. Whether anyone 'really' made a golem is the wrong question; the right one is what the tradition believed language could do — and what that belief did to its holders.

Textual state: the Yetzirah survives in multiple recensions (short, long, and Saadia's version) differing substantially — there is no single 'original' to appeal to. The critical reader compares recensions; the traditional reader follows one. Knowing which you're doing is the discipline.

example.code:
Sefer Yetzirah: the 32 paths (1:1)
  'With thirty-two wondrous paths of wisdom
   engraved Yah... He created His universe:
   ten sephiroth beli mah [out of nothing]
   and twenty-two letters.'
  The creative acts (verbs of making):
    chaqaq (engraved) -- chatzav (hewed) -- tzeraf (combined)
    shaqal (weighed) -- hemir (interchanged)
  Creation = combinatorial linguistics: permute the letters,
  and the world permutes with them.
example.walkthrough: The quoted opening establishes the 32 paths as the text's foundation, and the five verbs of making (engraved, hewed, combined, weighed, interchanged) show creation as craft operations on letters. The closing line states the doctrine baldly: combinatorial linguistics as cosmogony — the idea that will echo through Kabbalah, the golem legends, and eventually into computing's own combinatorics.

pitfalls: Quoting 'the' Yetzirah: the recensions differ substantially — cite which version (short/long/Saadia), or compare them.
Reading it as physics: it's cosmogony in a linguistic register, not a failed science text — judge it as metaphysics, not as engineering.
Golem literalism: the practical reading is commentarial tradition, not the text's plain sense — track which layer you're reading.
lessons.try_it: Read chapter 1 of the Sefer Yetzirah in translation (public domain versions exist). List the 32 paths as the text presents them, and note where the recensions you're comparing diverge.

lessons.title: The Sephiroth as Psychological Functions
concepts: The psychologized reading — developed by Jung, then by Dion Fortune, Gareth Knight, and the modern Qabalistic schools — maps the sephiroth onto structures of the psyche: Kether as the transcendent self, Chokmah/Binah as the intuitive/rational modes, Chesed/Geburah as the expansive/restrictive drives, Tiphareth as the integrated ego, Netzach/Hod as emotion/intellect, Yesod as the unconscious interface, Malkuth as embodied life.

The value of the mapping: it makes the Tree a diagnostic instrument — 'I'm stuck in unbalanced Geburah' names a recognizable state (rigidity, harsh judgment) and prescribes its complement (Chesed: deliberate generosity). The pillars become a theory of psychological balance with 500 years of symbolic vocabulary attached.

The cost of the mapping: it can reduce a theosophical system to self-help — the sephiroth become personality traits and the Tree a wellness diagram. The traditionalist objection has force: something is lost when Ein Sof becomes 'my higher self.' The serious student holds the psychological reading as one valid register among several, not the decoded truth.

Method: use the Tree diagnostically (which sephirah is over/under-active in this situation?), then check the reading against the traditional meanings — the friction between the registers is where the insight lives. A purely psychological Kabbalah and a purely theosophical one each miss half the instrument.

example.code:
Diagnostic use: the Tree as instrument
  Symptom ................. Tree reading ............ Prescription
  rigid judgment .......... Geburah unbalanced ..... deliberate Chesed acts
  boundary collapse ....... Chesed unbalanced ...... Geburah: say no, hold form
  racing thoughts ......... Hod overactive ........ Netzach: embody, endure
  numb disconnection ..... Yesod clouded ......... Malkuth: physical grounding
  grandiosity ............ Kether inflation ...... Tiphareth: human-scale work
example.walkthrough: The diagnostic table shows the psychologized Tree in action: symptoms mapped to sephirothic imbalances, each with a counterbalancing prescription from the opposite pillar. The walkthrough's point is methodological — use the Tree as an instrument, then check against traditional meanings; the productive friction between registers is the method, not a bug.

pitfalls: Reducing the Tree to therapy: the psychological register is one valid use, not the system's decoded truth — keep the theosophical register alive.
Diagnosing others: 'you're so unbalanced Geburah' as a weapon — the instrument is for self-work first; using it on others uninvited is a violation.
Skipping the traditional meanings: the diagnostic power comes from the symbol system's depth — shallow symbols give shallow diagnoses.
lessons.try_it: Take a current life situation and do a Tree diagnostic in writing: which sephirah is over/under-active, what does the opposite pillar prescribe, and what does the traditional meaning add to your reading?

lessons.title: Major Arcana: The Fool's Journey
concepts: The 22 Major Arcana (trumps) form a sequence from 0, The Fool, to XXI, The World — traditionally read as the Fool's journey: the soul's passage through archetypal stations. The Fool (innocence, the leap) meets the Magician (will, tools) and High Priestess (mystery, intuition), passes through the social archetypes (Empress, Emperor, Hierophant, Lovers), endures trials (Tower, Death, Devil, Moon), and arrives at integration (Sun, Judgment, World).

The journey is a reading technology, not a doctrine: a card's position in the sequence gives it neighbors and a narrative direction. The Tower (XVI) means something specific between the Devil (XV) and the Star (XVII) — catastrophe followed by hope. Readers who know the sequence read cards relationally; those who memorize keywords read them as isolated tokens.

The archetypes are deliberately multivalent — the Devil is bondage and also vitality, Death is ending and also transformation. The tradition's term is 'dignity': a card well- or ill-dignified by its neighbors and position. This built-in ambiguity is why Tarot resists both debunking ('it's vague') and dogmatism ('the Tower always means disaster').

Historical grounding: the trumps began as 15th-century Italian playing cards (tarocchi) — the esoteric meanings are an 18th–19th century overlay (de Gébelin, Lévi, the Golden Dawn). Knowing the gaming origin doesn't debunk the esoteric use; it dates it. The critical reader holds both: the cards are old, the system is modern.

example.code:
The Fool's journey (stations, abbreviated)
  0 Fool ......... the leap, innocence, beginnings
  I-VII .......... powers & society (Magician..Chariot)
  VIII-XIV ....... trials & virtues (Strength..Temperance)
  XV-XXI ......... ordeal & integration (Devil..World)
  Key turns: Tower (XVI) -- catastrophe; Star (XVII) -- hope;
             Moon (XVIII) -- illusion; Sun (XIX) -- clarity;
             Judgement (XX) -- reckoning; World (XXI) -- completion.
  Read cards by position in the journey, not as isolated keywords.
example.walkthrough: The station map shows the journey's arc — powers, trials, ordeal, integration — with the key turn from Tower through World spelled out as the sequence's emotional logic. The closing instruction is the method: relational reading via the journey versus keyword memorization. The historical note keeps the esoteric overlay dated honestly.

pitfalls: Keyword-memorizing the majors: isolated meanings miss the relational logic — learn the journey and read cards by station and neighbor.
Treating the esoteric meanings as ancient: the trumps are 15th-century game cards; the system is 18th-19th century — date the layers.
Single-meaning dogmatism: the cards are multivalent by design (dignities, reversals, positions) — certainty about 'what the Tower means' is the beginner's error.
lessons.try_it: Lay out the 22 majors in order. Narrate the Fool's journey aloud in your own words — one sentence per card. Note where your telling differs from book versions.

lessons.title: Minor Arcana: Pips & Court Cards
concepts: The 56 Minor Arcana mirror playing cards: four suits (Wands, Cups, Swords, Pentacles) of Ace through Ten, plus four court cards per suit (Page, Knight, Queen, King). The esoteric reading maps suits to elements (Wands-fire, Cups-water, Swords-air, Pentacles-earth) and numbers to sephirothic or Pythagorean meanings — the minors become a complete symbolic language, not just filler.

The pip-number system: each number 1–10 carries meaning (Ace: seed/potential, Two: balance/choice, Three: synthesis, ... Ten: completion/overfullness), modified by the suit's element. The Three of Cups (synthesis in water) reads as celebration/friendship; the Three of Swords (synthesis in air) as heartbreak — same number, different element, transformed meaning. Learn the numbers and elements and you can read any pip.

The court cards are the hard part — and the most useful: they represent people, personality facets, or approaches (the Knight of Swords as the hasty intellect, the Queen of Pentacles as nurturing practicality). The interpretive question is always 'person, part of self, or strategy?' — and the answer comes from the spread position and question, not the card alone.

Tradition note: the fully illustrated pips (every card a scene) are a Rider-Waite-Smith innovation (1909) — earlier decks (Marseille) show geometric pip arrangements, and readers read them numerologically. The illustrated pips teach faster; the Marseille pips teach deeper number-sense. Serious students eventually learn both.

example.code:
Reading any pip: number x element
  Numbers: 1 seed | 2 balance | 3 synthesis | 4 stability
             5 disruption | 6 harmony | 7 testing | 8 mastery
             9 fullness | 10 completion/overfull
  Elements: Wands=fire (will) | Cups=water (feeling)
              Swords=air (thought) | Pentacles=earth (matter)
  Example: 5 of Swords = disruption in thought -> conflict,
             hollow victory. 6 of Pentacles = harmony in matter
             -> generosity, balanced exchange.
example.walkthrough: The number-element matrix is the generative grammar of the minors: learn ten numbers and four elements and every pip becomes readable without memorization. The worked examples show the composition in action — the same number transformed by different elements. The tradition note dates the illustrated-pip innovation honestly.

pitfalls: Memorizing 56 separate meanings: the system is compositional — numbers times elements generates the meanings; memorize the grammar, not the dictionary.
Court cards as always-people: they can be people, personality facets, or strategies — the spread position disambiguates; defaulting to 'person' misses two-thirds of the readings.
Ignoring the Marseille pips: illustrated scenes are training wheels — the geometric pips build number-sense the pictures bypass.
lessons.try_it: Draw five random pips and read each from number × element without looking at the book meaning. Then check: where did the composition match, and where did the illustration add something?

lessons.title: Three Traditions: Marseille, Rider-Waite-Smith & Thoth
